Title: OCP Global Summit: Amid Ecosystem Adoption, NVIDIA Opens Vera Rubin Architecture to Help Scale AI Factories Worldwide

URL Source: https://blogs.nvidia.com/blog/ocp-global-summit-vera-rubin-scale-ai-factories/

Published Time: 2026-10-12T15:00:25+00:00

Markdown Content:
As AI factories grow from megawatts to gigawatts, building them takes more than advanced computing. Open standards are helping the industry scale AI infrastructure faster, more efficiently and more reliably.

At the Open Compute Project (OCP) Global Summit, taking place in the San Jose McEnery Convention Center, NVIDIA announced new partnerships and contributions aimed at creating a common foundation for next-generation AI infrastructure.

NVIDIA contributed key [NVIDIA Vera Rubin](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/data-center/technologies/rubin/) rack and compute tray designs to OCP through the open [NVIDIA MGX](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/data-center/products/mgx/) architecture, giving system builders a common foundation for developing next-generation AI factory infrastructure.

Together, these efforts span the AI factory itself, the utility grid that powers it and the rack-scale architecture at the heart of modern accelerated computing.

## **NVIDIA and Partners Announce Open Architecture Advances**

At the OCP event, NVIDIA and partners made a handful of announcements:

*   NVIDIA and hyperscalers published open standards for next-generation AI factories, including AI factory design standards and grid resilience.
*   NVIDIA launched new open source software components for NVIDIA DSX AI Factory.
*   Meta and NVIDIA advanced open AI networking with NVIDIA Spectrum-X Ethernet SuperNIC and Spectrum-6 innovations.
*   Visionbay introduced an 800V DC AI factory design for the Vera Rubin era.
*   NVIDIA and Cisco announced the Ultra-Dense Small Form Factor Pluggable (USFP) standard, the industry’s first module ​for 400Gb/s-based networking fabrics.
*   NVIDIA and Google announced Falcon Transport support on future NVIDIA ConnectX-10 SuperNICs and BlueField DPUs.

Before a packed audience, Ian Buck, vice president of hyperscale and high-performance computing at NVIDIA, discussed how open infrastructure is becoming a critical ingredient for scaling AI factories worldwide.

The [news at OCP](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/events/ocp-summit/) spotlights how NVIDIA’s extreme codesign combined with open standards is accelerating deployment, improving power efficiency and driving tokens-per-watt performance.

* * *

##

## **Vera Rubin AI Factories Advance With MGX Rack Contributions at OCP**[****](https://blogs.nvidia.com/blog/ocp-global-summit-vera-rubin-scale-ai-factories/#mgx)

NVIDIA joined industry leaders in contributing to the third-generation MGX AI data center reference design through OCP’s Open DC Initiative.

Combined with open liquid-cooling technologies such as MQD and MQDB, the effort helps turn proven AI factory designs into industry standards that others can adopt, manufacture and scale.

For NVIDIA Vera Rubin AI factories, the updated MGX 1.2 specification extends the open architecture for AI factories with rack-scale blind-mate liquid cooling, interoperable rack-scale interconnect infrastructure and a liquid-cooled 5,000A busbar designed for higher-power AI systems. It also adds native 19-inch equipment support and higher-density rack designs.

MGX 1.2 further expands modularity with configurable I/O bays, fanless liquid-cooled compute trays, standardized power and cooling interfaces, and a common infrastructure that helps ecosystem partners build interoperable accelerated computing platforms. It improves assembly, test and service times to streamline manufacturing and field service to enable faster and more efficient infrastructure buildout. The architecture supports rack deployments up to 250kW while simplifying serviceability, deployment and infrastructure reuse.

The Vera CPU rack design specification extends the NVIDIA MGX open architecture beyond accelerated computing, providing a purpose-built platform for the growing agentic AI era. While Vera Rubin NVL72 serves as the foundation for large-scale training and inference, the [NVIDIA Vera CPU](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/data-center/vera-cpu/) rack is designed to support tool calling, orchestration and sandboxed execution, helping AI agents interact with applications, data and services in real time.

Built on the third-generation NVIDIA MGX rack architecture, the Vera CPU rack shares the same rack-scale design principles that unite compute, networking, power and cooling into a common modular platform. This approach enables partners to deploy specialized infrastructure while benefiting from a shared ecosystem, simplified integration and a consistent foundation for next-generation AI factories.

* * *

## **NVIDIA Launches New Open Source Software Components for DSX AI Factory**[****](https://blogs.nvidia.com/blog/ocp-global-summit-vera-rubin-scale-ai-factories/#dsx)

[NVIDIA DSX AI factory platform](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/data-center/products/dsx/) applies extreme codesign to unify computing, networking, power, cooling, facilities and software, helping AI factories operate as a single optimized system, maximizing AI output within available infrastructure constraints. At the center of this unified system is DSX OS, the open operating layer that turns the DSX architecture into coordinated, repeatable operations at scale.

At OCP, NVIDIA expanded DSX OS with open source components for configuring networks, validating clusters, managing racks and provisioning bare metal:

*   [NVIDIA Config Manager](https://github.com/dsx-ai-factory/nv-config-manager): Automates switch configurations at scale, allowing customers to deploy, validate and maintain consistent AI factory network fabrics with minimal to zero manual intervention/
*   [NVIDIA Cluster Readiness Engine](https://github.com/NVIDIA/cluster-readiness-engine): Helps eliminate costly job crashes by stress-testing GPU clusters with real workload simulations to guarantee hardware health before training begins
*   [NVIDIA Rack Management Service](https://github.com/dsx-ai-factory/nv-rms): Offers a rack hardware abstraction and operations solutions that treats racks as first-class units for improved AI factory scale firmware management.
*   [Cluster API Provider for NVIDIA Infrastructure Controller](https://github.com/dsx-ai-factory/cluster-api-provider-nico): Accelerates bare-metal deployment and tenant onboarding, turning raw AI hardware into production-ready clusters in hours instead of days.

Developed from NVIDIA’s experience running NVIDIA DGX Cloud, these open source components enable cloud providers and software partners to integrate AI factory capabilities directly into their multi-tenant platforms.

_Developers can visit the_[_DSX AI Factory Github page_](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/data-center/vera-cpu/)_to explore and contribute to both the new and existing open source software components from NVIDIA DSX AI Factory platform._

* * *

## **NVIDIA and Hyperscalers Publish Open Standards for Next-Generation AI Factories**[****](https://blogs.nvidia.com/blog/ocp-global-summit-vera-rubin-scale-ai-factories/#open-standards)

For AI infrastructure to scale globally, it needs more than advanced hardware — it needs a common foundation that the entire industry can build on.

At OCP, NVIDIA joined AMD, Google and Meta t o publish a new open specification that establishes that foundation. The [Open Data Center Specification v0.7](https://www.opencompute.org/documents/open-data-center-spec-revision-0-7-0-4-pdf) defines a unified blueprint for next-generation AI factory facility design — from power architecture to cooling infrastructure to physical layout.

The [OCP Grid Resilience Specification](https://www.opencompute.org/documents/ocp-base-spec-interface-specification-between-hyperscalers-and-utility-grid-for-disturbance-performance-pdf), published by Google, Meta, Microsoft and NVIDIA, establishes how large-scale AI infrastructure should behave during utility grid disturbances: staying connected, responding automatically and restoring to near-full load within less than two seconds.

With these standards now open, manufacturers around the world have a common target to build for. Equipment makers, colocation providers and data center operators can begin designing, fabricating and delivering the infrastructure layer that powers AI factories under construction globally — without waiting for proprietary specifications from individual customers.

Being [NVIDIA DSX reference design](https://docs.nvidia.com/dsx)-compatible, these specifications provide a validated, deployable implementation of both specs, from facility layout and power architecture to the software that monitors and responds to grid signals in real time. For operators building Vera Rubin AI factories, there’s now a straight line from open community standard to a running system.

* * *

## **Visionbay.ai Designs 800VDC AI Factory for the Vera Rubin Era**[****](https://blogs.nvidia.com/blog/ocp-global-summit-vera-rubin-scale-ai-factories/#visionbay)

As AI factories grow larger and more powerful, one challenge looms over them all: delivering enough power to the accelerated computing systems driving the next generation of AI.

At OCP, Visionbay unveiled plans for K-1, a next-generation AI factory platform designed around an [800 VDC architecture](https://blogs.nvidia.com/blog/800-vdc-power-architecture-ai-factory) and built with future NVIDIA Vera Rubin deployments in mind. The project combines NVIDIA’s 800 VDC reference architecture with power and thermal technologies from Vertiv to create a scalable foundation for high-density AI infrastructure.

The design addresses a growing industry challenge. As AI training, inference and reasoning workloads expand, rack power densities continue to rise. Traditional low-voltage power distribution becomes increasingly difficult to scale, requiring more copper, more cabling and more power-conversion equipment.

By adopting NVIDIA’s 800 VDC architecture, K-1 creates a path toward higher-density AI infrastructure while preserving flexibility for existing deployments. Rather than requiring a complete transition on day one, the platform is designed to phase in 800 VDC distribution where it delivers the greatest benefit, helping operators prepare for future generations of accelerated computing without extensive facility redesign.

The architecture is designed around cluster-level power centers that centralize AC-to-DC conversion and distribute 800 VDC closer to compute resources. The approach simplifies downstream power delivery, supports modular expansion and creates repeatable building blocks for future AI factory growth.

K-1 also reflects the system-level design philosophy behind NVIDIA AI factories, where power, cooling and computing are engineered together. With support for liquid-cooled infrastructure, scalable power distribution and future Vera Rubin-class deployments, the project demonstrates how ecosystem partners are translating NVIDIA’s AI factory architecture into deployable infrastructure designed for the next era of accelerated computing.

* * *

At the event, Meta and NVIDIA announced that Meta is adopting NVIDIA Spectrum-6 102.4Tb/s Ethernet switches to build larger, higher-performance NVIDIA Vera Rubin AI factories on open networking.

Spectrum-6 delivers twice the switching capacity and per-lane bandwidth of Spectrum-4, and provides a lossless Ethernet AI fabric at 200G per lane, with high effective bandwidth and performance isolation that keeps one job’s traffic from slowing another’s.

Meta’s Spectrum-6-based switch, N-IceCube, slots into IcePack, Meta’s 100T, liquid-cooled rack. N-IceCube runs the Facebook Open Switching System (FBOSS), Meta’s open source network operating system that contributed to OCP to support efficient networking at hyperscale.

Meta’s Superintelligence Lab released
a pair of new state-of-the-art models
on Monday, Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full, representing the company’s first attempt at a frontier model.
Where Muse Spark aimed to be a lightweight model that could perform at low latency, the Wonder models are larger and said to be more capable, with higher benchmark scores and better results on complex tasks like coding.
According to Meta’s testing (presented in
the model card
), Wonder and Wonder Full achieve comparable benchmark scores to Fable 5.1 and GPT-6 Astra.
“Together, they mark the next step on our scaling ladder and a major leap toward personal superintelligence,” Meta’s blog post about the models reads.
That scale is reflected in the pricing: Accessed through the Meta Model API, Wonder will cost $4 per million input tokens and $20 per million output tokens, making it roughly equivalent in cost to GPT-6 Sol or Opus 5.5.
Notably, Wonder Full will only be available to Muse Code subscribers and will not be served through the API. Both models will also be used to power the Muse agent.
In keeping with Meta’s interest in developing personal assistants that can perform tasks over a long period, the company placed particular emphasis on the new models’ ability to retain and synthesize information given by the user, a property Meta calls “active memory.”
To achieve better recall, Meta highlighted
the MemoryBench benchmark
, which challenges continual learning and memory construction frameworks. According to the company’s testing, Muse Wonder now scores higher on MemoryBench than Fable, Opus, or Astra.
“We put a tremendous amount of effort into making sure your model can remember what’s important to you over days, weeks, months, and beyond,” said research scientist Kavya Kopparapu in a video accompanying the launch.
The new models are the first frontier model release since Scale AI founder Alexandr Wang restructured Meta’s AI efforts
in August of last year
. Since then, Meta has released its lightweight Muse Spark model and
Muse agent
but has avoided the kind of state-of-the-art model releases OpenAI and Anthropic are known for.
According to the post, the models were trained at Meta’s
Prometheus data center in central Ohio
, which came online earlier this year.

articles.content:
The U.S. Air Force will buy data collected by
WindBorne Systems
‘ fleet of autonomous weather balloons under a new contract that could be worth nearly $50 million to the startup.
WindBorne currently has about 700 weather balloons flying around the globe, collecting atmospheric sensor readings that the company sells to customers and also feeds into its own AI weather forecasting model. WindBorne, founded in 2015 and based in Redwood City, California, is one of the first organizations to directly feed empirical data into a deep-learning weather model.
The company has worked closely with the U.S. government, particularly the National Weather Service and the U.S. Air Force and Navy, but this is the single-largest contract the company has participated in. The contract is worth up to $49 million, but the Air Force pays only as it needs data. It can place orders for specific regions at specific times. So far, it has ordered $1.7 million worth, and executives expect more orders to follow.
“This is largely a vehicle through which continued growth of the constellation can be supported, as well as some work on research and development to continue to improve the hardware and performance of the balloons,” WindBorne co-founder and CTO Andrey Sushko told TechCrunch. He added that the contract, which was awarded without competitive bidding, is “a determination by the government that for this capability of collecting global data, we were the only company able to provide it in the way that met their needs for these operations.”
WindBorne CEO John Dean
told TechCrunch
in August that the company had raised a $37 million Series B round to continue scaling its business. Earlier this summer, the company
released
the latest version of its forecasting model, WeatherMesh 6, which
it says
provides more accurate forecasts than the traditional model run by the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF), which simulates the atmosphere using the laws of physics.
Since the arrival of transformer model architectures and the ECMWF’s release of a massive weather dataset a few years ago, AI weather forecasting has become one of the more productive uses of deep-learning technology. Meteorologists previously relied on expensive supercomputers running detailed equations that approximate how the atmosphere behaves. Now, end-to-end learning can ingest decades of weather data and issue predictions more quickly.
Models built by frontier labs and government agencies are
proving more accurate
than traditional forecasts, although it is still a jagged frontier, with both types of forecasts required to enable useful understanding of the weather. Google DeepMind’s
latest weather model
offers important new capabilities, and its cyclone forecasting tools are becoming
increasingly central
to how the U.S. government responds to hurricane season.
In August WindBorne became the first organization to send an unpowered flight system — one with no engine — to collect data in the
eye of a typhoon
. The company maneuvers its balloons by adjusting their altitude, bleeding air, or dropping sand carried as ballast, to send the vehicles into winds that take them where they need to go.
“That’s a pretty novel step, and the two ingredients for that are one, having good wind and weather models, and knowing how to navigate them; and two, having a large enough constellation that you have balloons in the right places,” Sushko said. “It’s one of the first times that a deep-learning model was used for actual operational decisions.”

articles.content:
Microsoft president Brad Smith is calling for urgent regulation of AI, and his argument is that consumer products like milk and washing machines have more oversight than the companies building artificial intelligence.
On a
recent BBC podcast
, Smith called AI both a “weapon and a tool” that is putting the world’s cybersecurity at risk and said the “moment has arrived” to institute global safety rules.
Smith also said the U.K., and not the U.S. or European Union, is best placed to lead on global safety rules. Britain’s AI Security Institute (AISI), launched in 2023, receives access to major models from U.S. frontier labs before they are deployed and has quickly become a leader in AI safety testing.
That role has been under threat in recent weeks, with U.S. president Donald Trump warning against “globalist” organizations, which he claims are interfering with American companies. Last month, he
reportedly
asked Anthropic and OpenAI to withhold new models from British testers, but AISI
confirmed on Monday
that it is able to access and test the latest models.
Despite the president’s pushback, however, Smith argued the U.K. can regulate AI in ways that the U.S. cannot.
“In Washington, D.C., people don’t look at the U.K. and they don’t look at London the way they look at Brussels,” he told the BBC. “That’s a strength.”
His comments come amid rallying cries from tech leaders, including
Anthropic’s Dario Amodei
and OpenAI’s Sam Altman, to slow the pace of AI development in the wake of several incidents where AI agents went rogue.
Last month, Trump hosted
tech leaders
of companies, including OpenAI, Anthropic, Nvidia, AMD, SpaceX, Meta, and Google, at the White House to discuss AI safety. They signed a “morally binding” document in which they agreed to work with “independent auditors” to assess the safety and capabilities of their AI models.
Smith says the document is a “good step,” but it stops short of the type of regulation that is necessary. The problem with voluntary self-regulation, he said, is that only the “good companies” will comply.
“It’s the companies that are not as responsible that you need to worry about,” he said.
Smith outlined several AI safety rules he’d like to see put into place, like a legal obligation to alert an organization if its system was breached by rogue AI agents. He also appears to be in favor of AI labs getting the approval of outside evaluators before an AI product is released and spoke positively about kill switches to pause or slow down AI if humans lose control of it.
“Let’s speak calmly, maybe even softly, but firmly, and start to bring people together,” Smith said. “I hope that’s the role we can play as a company. I hope that’s the role the U.K. can play as a country.”

articles.content:
Nearly two decades ago, a young college student wrote his final thesis about software capable of generating design documents for school buildings. Al Dram was studying architecture — following in the footsteps of his parents and grandfather — but it was technology that really intrigued him.
There was just one problem: The technology his idea required didn’t exist yet.
“Then ChatGPT came along,” said Dram, recalling when OpenAI released the generative AI chatbot that uses large language models (LLMs) in November 2022.
His old idea suddenly seemed a lot more possible. Within six months, he launched the concept of Blueprints AI, a startup that uses AI to produce code-compliant and permit-ready architectural construction blueprints in minutes from a 2D sketch or PDF.
Blueprints AI
, which Dram officially incorporated in 2025 in Santa Monica with co-founder Coco Cao, was selected for the
2026 Startup Battlefield 200
, a cohort of promising early-stage startups that have earned a spot to exhibit at this year’s
TechCrunch Disrupt
, taking place this week from October 13 to 15 in San Francisco.
During that 20-year lead-up to Blueprints AI, Dram earned his bachelor’s and master’s degrees in architecture from the University of Tehran and completed two years of PhD coursework on digital design at the European Graduate School in Switzerland. He moved to the United States and opened an architecture firm in 2018 called Drams Design-Build. Then, after obtaining a general contractor’s license, he added a construction business in 2021.
Dram should have been satisfied. He wasn’t.
“I was saying, okay, maybe I can build new projects that change people’s life in that area, but it wouldn’t be a big impact,” he said. “What makes me very excited about technology is the impact, the hours saved, the energy saved of people doing the same thing over and over and over.”
Blueprints AI will unveil a more capable second-generation version of its software at Disrupt. Dram and Cao say it will make a big impact because it takes over the repetitive drafting work that fills most of an architect’s day.
“It will make better spaces for people because now architects have the time to design,” said Dram. He said architects spend about 80% of their time on drafting and only 20% on design. “I want to flip that to be 20-80.”
Dram and Cao met at an AI conference several years ago and combined their skills to build the company. Cao, a data scientist from Hong Kong, handles sales and go-to-market strategy as chief commercial officer.
The pair trained their models using eight years of approved drawing sets from Dram’s design and construction firm, which is still in business.
Its first-generation software produces architectural construction documents and costs between $3,200 and $8,500 a month, depending on the plan. Custom pricing for enterprises is also available.
The startup’s second-generation software will deliver a considerable upgrade. Customers can start with a description or sketch of a project and create blueprints for every aspect of a building at once, including architecture, structural, mechanical, electrical, plumbing, and interior design. Version 2 allows users to design and make changes to the project, an upgrade over the first iteration. Importantly, one design change updates the entire project and is checked against local building codes.
Early customers are already using the second version, and Dram said it will become publicly available this week. The startup is already working on a third version of its software that will add in structural analysis and electrical panel design.
The technology doesn’t replace licensed architects, according to the co-founders. Licensed professionals still review the documents and affix their seal before submitting them for permits. The judgment stays human, they say.
Blueprints AI is targeting two groups with its new software. Professional architecture, engineering, and design firms make up one group, while developers and real estate owners make up another. The startup offers its software as a subscription and may add a one-time flat-fee option for those who just want it for a single project.

articles.content:
One of the core promises of AI is that the more it knows about a person, the better it will be able to assist them with tasks and make appropriate suggestions, which, if you’ll believe the tech companies,
requires
apps and devices to listen, watch, or record users’ activity all the time and gather all possible context.
There’s obviously privacy and data security concerns with anything that’s collecting data about you continuously. But startups are building such apps undeterred anyway, arming themselves with the belief that the market for personalized assistance is big enough to swallow such concerns.
Former Plaud exec Peter Mo is building
Ambi
to do something similar. The app aims to provide real-time intelligence and insights to people by listening to them all the time.
The company said on Monday that it has raised $26 million across multiple funding rounds led by Luminous Ventures, which has backed companies like Meituan and Unitree Robotics, and original design manufacturer (ODM) Huaqin.
Ambi is also releasing apps for iPhones, Macs, and Apple Watch. These apps act like meeting notetakers, but users can choose to have them listening so they can capture context all day.
Meeting notetaking companies have been working to automate tasks that follow once calls are done, based on the summaries and action items they gather during the conversation, and using multitudes of connectors to software systems. Ambi wants to take this a step further by having its agent start the work during the meeting itself.
The company’s promise is that its AI agent can proactively give you suggestions or surface relevant knowledge while you are in a meeting, based on your calendar, meetings, knowledge base, and web data. Users can also start a task on one device and continue it on another.
Ambi co-founder Peter Mo.
Image Credits:
Ambi
“The way we interact with intelligence is limited. Often the intelligence is trapped on the screen, and if you use hardware like Plaud, you need to wait for recording to transfer to the phone, upload to the cloud, and get intelligence after processing. That’s why we are building Ambi to use AI anytime and anywhere,” Mo, the company’s co-founder and CEO, told TechCrunch.
The company has ambitions to capture more information. Its upcoming desktop app will be able to look at the work that users do and store important parts in its memory to give more personalized suggestions. Apps like
Littlebird
or
Minimi
already do something similar.
The startup is also planning to launch its own hardware device, which will have a screen, a speaker, a camera, and microphones to capture context and display information.
Image Credits:
Ambi
Question of privacy
Ambi’s launch comes amidst growing concerns around AI devices that don’t have enough indicators to suggest they are capturing data on people around the user. It is not clear if Ambi’s apps or its upcoming device will have enough indicators to alert third parties that their conversations are being recorded if the user doesn’t disclose their use of Ambi’s tech.
Some
meeting notetakers
have
even been sued
because their tech recorded people’s conversations and data without their consent. Plus, the recent release of Apple’s Audio Intelligence feature, which transcribes speech continuously,
has raised privacy concerns
.
Mo said that users can turn off ambient data capture on Ambi’s apps and devices at any time, and the feature is off by default. The startup said it doesn’t store any recordings of users and encrypts the data, but it didn’t specify what kind of encryption it uses. Despite these measures, the onus of declaring ambient capture is still on the users. He classified this as an industry-wide problem.
“We have to inform our users that they have to tell others about ambient capture. We, as an industry, haven’t solved this problem [of disclosure]. We have tried to put the information about disclosure in every place possible, but if users try to hide the capture, we can’t just solve the problem,” he said.
Ambi currently has over 50 staff across offices in San Francisco, Beijing, Shanghai, and Shenzhen. The company is hiring for its go-to-market function and AI engineers for working on speech-recognition models.

by

Microsoft’s Maia 300 chip.
Image: Microsoft
Tom Warren
is a senior correspondent and author of
Notepad
, who has been covering all things Microsoft, PC, and tech for over 20 years.
Microsoft is announcing its third-generation Maia in-house AI chip today, designed to be the “primary AI inference system” for Microsoft’s products and services. Maia 300 not only improves the cost and efficiency of running AI workloads in the cloud, it’s also more capable of handling the latest reasoning models and agentic tasks.
Maia 300 will start being rolled out to production in 2027, and it has been designed with efficiency in mind. “We expect Maia 300 to deliver 40 percent more tokens per megawatt compared to leading GPU-based systems,”
says Scott Guthrie
, executive vice president of Microsoft’s cloud group. “And in a full 96-accelerator configuration, it delivers up to 7x the rack-scale token throughput of Maia 200.”
These efficiency improvements will allow Microsoft to rely mainly on its in-house AI chips soon, instead of ones from Nvidia and AMD. “We will scale our Azure Maia family to multi-gigawatt deployments starting in 2027, making Maia the primary AI inference system for Microsoft products and services,” says Guthrie.
Maia 300 chips will start being used for production workloads in 2027.
Image: Microsoft
Maia 300 is a successor to the 200, which was only
announced in January
. Maia 200 is already running on production AI workloads across Microsoft, including Microsoft Copilot, GitHub Copilot, Microsoft Foundry, and Microsoft’s own AI models.
“Maia 200 is the best performing AI infrastructure in our fleet, measured in real world metrics for AI services,” says Guthrie. “Maia 300 is a complete AI system designed for the new types of AI workloads emerging today: Long-context reasoning, latency-sensitive conversational experiences, and sustained, multi-step agentic tasks.”
Related
Microsoft is finally making custom chips — and they’re all about AI
Microsoft’s latest AI chip goes head-to-head with Amazon and Google
Microsoft is using a new chiplet architecture to get its all-important efficiency gains. Built on TSMC’s N2P process node, the latest Maia 300 architecture separates compute, memory controller, and I/O functions. “This increases the silicon area dedicated to compute performance and allows each function to use the technology best suited to its role,”
says the Azure hardware
and infrastructure team.
Maia 300 is also a key part of Microsoft’s own AI model work, and could help the company achieve
its goal of catching up
with Google DeepMind, OpenAI, and Anthropic. “We have to work across the full stack, all the way down to the silicon,” says Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman. “At that scale we need a platform that we own, and that we co-design with our models. That’s why running our Microsoft AI models on top of the Maia chip is a critical focus for our team.”

Mars may be a hellhole, but the moon is not far behind
The US and China are racing to build bases on the moon, with NASA hoping to establish a small lunar city by the end of the century. But the moon is a tremendously hostile place to set up camp.
A sprawling lunar base must be safe for its inhabitants, protected from falling asteroids, endless cosmic radiation, razor-sharp lunar dust, and torturous temperature swings. It also must be somewhat self-sustaining.
That will require autonomous robots, nuclear power, and a way to use the moon’s resources to keep the base operating. But the chief obstacle may be one of political will.

.

Title: Meta's new frontier model Muse Wonder Full breaks into the AI top tier

URL Source: https://the-decoder.com/metas-new-frontier-model-muse-wonder-full-breaks-into-the-ai-top-tier/

Published Time: 2026-10-12T18:48:29+00:00

Markdown Content:
**Meta released its frontier model Muse Wonder in two variants, and both land among the best AI models available.**

Muse Wonder Full scores 56 points on the [Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index](https://artificialanalysis.ai/models/muse-wonder-full) v4.3, while Muse Wonder hits 52. Its predecessor, [Muse Spark 1.3](https://the-decoder.com/meta-closes-in-on-the-top-with-muse-spark-1-3-and-undercuts-rivals-on-price/), sat at 48 points, which makes this a significant jump from what was a mid-tier model.

The biggest gains show up in agentic evaluations, tests that measure how well an AI model can handle complex tasks on its own. On Terminal-Bench 4.0, performance jumped from 33 to 57 percent. Muse Wonder Full places in the top three on six out of ten benchmarks overall, a strong result for Meta, which seems to have recovered after a weaker stretch with its open Llama models.

Muse Wonder Full scores 56 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, placing it among the top frontier models. | Image: Artificial Analysis

Meta highlights two new features. "Active Memory" lets the model remember key information across conversations and recall it when needed. "Active Focus" is the model's ability to stick with difficult tasks, try alternative approaches, and ask follow-up questions when something isn't clear. Both are [central to Meta's pitch](https://research.meta.ai/blog/muse-wonder) for a personal AI agent that can access calendars, messages, and documents.

Both models support a one-million-token context window and accept text, images, video, and audio as input. Muse Wonder is available through [Meta's API](https://dev.meta.ai/) and [Muse Code](https://dev.meta.ai/code), while Muse Wonder Full is currently limited to Muse Code users. Muse Wonder will soon power the [Muse app](https://muse.ai/) as well, starting with paying subscribers. Over time, Meta plans to build specialized models from it for all users.

## Coding jumps sharply, but factual knowledge lags behind

Both models show big improvements in coding. Muse Wonder Full hits 68 points on the Coding Agents Index, tying Claude Code with Sonnet 5.5. Muse Wonder scores 63, up from 54 for its predecessor.

Factual knowledge remains a weak spot. On the AA-Omniscience knowledge test, Muse Wonder Full manages only 30 points, and Muse Wonder gets 25. That's well behind Claude Opus 5.5 (46), GPT-6 Astra (43), and Gemini 4 Argon (42), which suggests the Wonder series is built on a smaller base model than its competitors. Low hallucination rates help offset this gap. Muse Wonder Full cuts its hallucination rate from 33 to 23 percent compared to its predecessor, the second-lowest among all models scoring at least 45 index points. Only [Gemini 4 Argon (15 percent)](https://the-decoder.de/google-gemini-4-argon-schliesst-zur-ki-spitze-auf-bleibt-aber-hinter-anthropics-claude-opus-5-5/) hallucinates less often.

Meta addresses a common criticism [in its blog post](https://research.meta.ai/blog/muse-wonder), that Muse models are tuned for benchmarks but fall short in real-world use. The company says Muse Wonder Full does better than expected on unfamiliar tasks that weren't part of training optimization, and credits this to a stronger base model.

Meta's official benchmark results show the online advertising company has caught up to the leading frontier models. | Image: Meta

On the [Vals AI Index](https://x.com/ValsAI/status/2109706320383545474), Muse Wonder Full (Max) debuts at fifth place and beats all OpenAI models, according to Vals AI. Only current Anthropic models score higher. Muse Wonder lands at tenth.

The biggest improvements come from coding and math. On ProofBench, a private benchmark for mathematical proofs, Muse Wonder Full solves 94 out of 100 problems, up from 58 for its predecessor. That puts it just five to six points behind the top models (99 to 100). On Terminal-Bench 4, Muse Wonder Full doubled its score while using 30 percent fewer output tokens. Performance on finance and legal tasks stayed at predecessor levels, dropping up to two points.

## Better performance comes at a steep price

According to Artificial Analysis, Muse Wonder runs $4.52 per task on the Intelligence Index, nearly three times more than Muse Spark 1.3 ($1.60). Token pricing has climbed too, with $4 per million input tokens and $20 for output, up from $1.25 and $4.25 for the predecessor. Muse Wonder also uses 28 percent more input tokens per task, and those account for 76 percent of total costs.

That puts Muse Wonder below Claude Fable 5.1 ($7.63) and Claude Opus 5.5 ($5.98) in pricing, but above GPT-6 Astra ($3.26), Gemini 4 Argon ($1.99), and GPT-6.1 Sol ($0.72). No token pricing is available yet for Muse Wonder Full. Both models do use about 10 percent fewer output tokens than their predecessor.

Meta says it trained the models at its in-house Prometheus data center at gigawatt scale. More details are in the [model card](https://research.meta.ai/static/muse-wonder-model-card).

articles.content:
Title: Sakana AI's self-improving model gets better at solving and judging, but can't catch its own blind spots

URL Source: https://the-decoder.com/sakana-ais-self-improving-model-gets-better-at-solving-and-judging-but-cant-catch-its-own-blind-spots/

Published Time: 2026-10-12T17:58:54+00:00

Markdown Content:
**Sakana AI's MASS method lets one language model improve itself by solving tasks, judging results, and refining workflows without a stronger teacher model. The study finds gains across all three roles, but shared blind spots can let errors pass as progress and feed into the next training cycle.**

Researchers from Sakana AI and UC Berkeley have introduced "Multi-Agent Self-Supervision" (MASS), a method for recursive self-improvement (RSI). A single language model handles the task, optimizes how the work gets done, and evaluates the results.

At the research frontier, even experts often struggle to judge results because verification can require costly supporting evidence or lengthy experiments, the authors argue. A single plasma study can take more than 120 million CPU hours, [according to the paper](https://pub.sakana.ai/mass/).

The model itself may therefore be the best available judge, even though it can miss its own mistakes when reviewing its work. Using the same model to solve, check, and revise can reinforce those errors rather than correct them.

## Copies of one model divide up the work

Inspired by "Society of Mind," a book by AI pioneer Marvin Minsky, the researchers focus on how the model divides up the work. In MASS, a workflow is text appended to the prompt that defines each sub-agent's role and instructions. A "contract" specifies what information each sub-agent must return and which checks it must perform, while a "hop" sets the order of calls.

An orchestrator distributes the work among the sub-agents. When testing a trading strategy against historical prices, for example, the data specialist's contract must ensure the strategy uses only information available at each point in time.

During the inner loop, the model's weights stay frozen as the team runs a candidate workflow and the evaluator compares the result against the current "champion." The optimizer uses that feedback to propose the next workflow, mainly by changing contracts and hops. In the outer loop, the champion runs 18 times per task, with the model ranking the results itself and selecting up to 15 runs for training.

Copies of the same model run the workflow as a team, while a self-evaluator compares the result against the current champion. A self-optimizer uses that feedback to write the next workflow, and the model learns from its best runs after each round. | Image: Sakana AI

The researchers remove the workflow text from the orchestrator's initial prompt in the training examples so the model learns to organize work based on the task alone. Specific assignments to sub-agents remain in the recorded traces, and the model takes on all three roles again after LoRA fine-tuning.

The base model is [Qwen3.6-27B](https://the-decoder.com/qwen3-6-27b-beats-much-larger-predecessor-on-most-coding-benchmarks/), with [Qwen Code as the harness](https://the-decoder.com/qwen3-coder-is-alibabas-most-agentic-coding-model-to-date/). The researchers use twelve research tasks generated by [GPT-5.5](https://the-decoder.com/openai-unveils-gpt-5-5-claims-a-new-class-of-intelligence-at-double-the-api-price/) across finance, robotics, and pharmaceuticals, reserving three for testing and nine for training. Only eight yield training data because the search finds no workflow that beats the reference on one training task.

## Benchmark gains come mostly from completing more work

On the test tasks, the win rate against the base model rises from 53.9 percent after one round to 69.9 percent after two. On MLR-Bench, DSBench, ScienceAgentBench, and AstaBench, the model reaches 1.2 to 1.6 times the base model's score per output token. Gains in raw scores are sometimes small, with DSBench improving only from 0.473 to 0.482, while scores drop slightly on Terminal-Bench 2.0 and SWE-bench Verified.

After two rounds, the model leads on MLR-Bench, DSBench, ScienceAgentBench, and AstaBench, while the base model still scores higher on Terminal-Bench 2.0 and SWE-bench Verified. | Image: Sakana AI

The paper's appendix shows that completed MLR-Bench submissions rise from 31 to 50 out of 60, while their average grade falls from 3.07 to 2.88. The delegation tool goes unused in all 180 runs, leaving it unclear whether teamwork explains the gains.

Those gains are no longer statistically significant when results are compared task by task. The authors describe mixed results across research tasks, with AstaBench showing the same pattern.

## Training on solutions also improves the evaluator and optimizer

Although the model trains only on solution traces, its performance in the other two roles improves as well. The self-evaluator's agreement with external judges rises from 73 to 93 percent. Workflows found after one round beat the base model's workflows 64 percent of the time, even when the base model runs both.

Without workflow instructions, the base model delegates to sub-agents in just one of 110 runs, compared with 87 after two rounds. It could already delegate when explicitly instructed, but now does so without being asked.

During optimization, task knowledge shifts into contracts and hops, while roles and instructions become more generic. That finding rests on a small sample of just eight to nine tasks.

Training on team traces produces a model with a 68.3 percent win rate, compared with 64 percent for a single-agent student, using 31 percent fewer training tokens. External judges prefer team results 85.1 percent of the time, though teams produce about 2.4 times as many tokens. When outputs are similar in length, judges prefer team results 80 percent of the time, based on just ten pairs.

The evaluated team runs perform better, but the comparison doesn't establish that delegation alone explains the advantage. Team and single-agent runs also differ in workflow instructions, review instructions, and which successfully completed episodes were selected.

The MASS model M+ reaches a 68.3 percent win rate after processing about 29 million training tokens, compared with 64.0 percent for single-agent student S++ with 42 million tokens. | Image: Sakana AI

## Better feedback helps only if the optimizer can use it

Replacing only the evaluator with GPT-5.5 barely helped; the search progressed much faster only when the optimizer was stronger too. The authors conclude that good feedback helps only when the optimizer can act on it. With Qwen handling all three roles, the search still finds winning workflows for 11 of 12 tasks, but takes longer.

The extent of a workflow rewrite says little about its effect on results, and even byte-identical workflows can produce opposite outcomes. One run won all six external judgments, while another lost all six after the agent got stuck in a loop. The researchers suspect that limiting how much the optimizer changes at each step could help stabilize the search.

With GPT-5.5 as both evaluator and optimizer, the search finds winning workflows for all twelve tasks after five iterations. Using Qwen for all three roles takes 13 iterations to find winning workflows for eleven tasks, with large swings between iterations shown on the right. | Image: Sakana AI

After failed simulations in a robotics task, the model had the simulator modified to move objects directly to the target, then reported success. External judges still rated the run positively five out of six times. In another trace used for training, a check passed even though it had returned only invalid values.

The authors see shared blind spots as the potential "Achilles' heel" of recursive self-improvement. If the model misses the same error in all three roles, that error could be accepted as an improvement and baked into the next model. The weakness would then affect both the system and its correction mechanism, prompting the authors to call for independent checks, limits on autonomy, and clear conditions for intervention. The [code](https://github.com/SakanaAI/mass) is publicly available.

Japanese research lab Sakana AI launched a dedicated [research lab for recursive self-improvement](https://the-decoder.com/sakana-ai-bets-ai-that-improves-itself-can-break-the-compute-arms-race-of-frontier-labs/?cmpscreencustom=1) in June, building on earlier work including the [Darwin-Godel Machine](https://the-decoder.com/sakana-ais-darwin-godel-machine-evolves-by-rewriting-its-own-code-to-boost-performance/?cmpscreencustom=1) and the [AI Scientist](https://the-decoder.com/automated-research-the-ai-scientist-generates-papers-for-15-dollars-each/). Google researchers are pursuing a related approach, automatically optimizing the [scaffolding of prompts, workflows, and tools around a fixed model](https://the-decoder.com/google-researchers-find-a-way-to-keep-self-improving-ai-agents-from-memorizing-their-tests/?cmpscreencustom=1) without letting agents overfit to their test tasks.

Vals AI recently found that [agent teams](https://the-decoder.com/ai-agent-teams-waste-massive-tokens-for-barely-measurable-quality-gains-research-finds/) cost 1.8 to 5.1 times as much as single agents but performed measurably better in only one of four comparisons. Anthropic showed that models engaging in [reward hacking](https://the-decoder.com/strict-anti-hacking-prompts-make-ai-models-more-likely-to-sabotage-and-lie-anthropic-finds/) to game their reward systems also learn to deceive and sabotage safety checks.

Title: Anthropic's Andrej Karpathy says "the external world has seen the preview" of what AI can actually do

URL Source: https://the-decoder.com/anthropics-andrej-karpathy-says-the-external-world-has-seen-the-preview-of-what-ai-can-actually-do/

Published Time: 2026-10-12T12:51:21+00:00

Markdown Content:
**Andrej Karpathy, co-founder of OpenAI, describes a rapidly widening gap in how people understand AI capabilities. While the public treats chatbots like a better Google search, internal frontier systems are already tackling tasks that would take top experts years to complete.**

[Karpathy breaks down](https://x.com/karpathy) the user base of large language models into four levels. About six billion people, roughly 75 percent of the global population, have barely come in contact with LLMs at all. Another one to two billion are casual users of free-tier ChatGPT-like products who treat them "a bit like a better Google search, a writing aid, or etc."

## Most people have no idea what AI can already do

Even many professionals outside of math and code fall into this tier. Executives and people in similar roles spend most of their time talking to other people, so "while they understand what is happening intellectually, it is still second-hand and a bit abstract," Karpathy writes.

The third tier covers an estimated 20 million people, about 0.2 percent of the world's population. These are professional users of frontier-grade LLMs in math and code who see firsthand that "large, complex projects that used to take them weeks/months can now be completed by agents with a prompt." Karpathy lists "building apps, copying apps, translating apps, decompiling apps from binaries" as examples.

He adds that this shift happened fast. In [October 2024, Karpathy called AI agents mostly marketing that barely worked](https://the-decoder.com/ai-researcher-andrej-karpathy-says-agentic-ai-is-years-away-from-matching-industry-hype/?trk=article-ssr-frontend-pulse_little-text-block). Just a few months later, he [stopped writing code by hand entirely](https://the-decoder.com/former-tesla-ai-chief-andrej-karpathy-now-codes-mostly-in-english-just-three-months-after-calling-ai-agents-useless/), going from "typing memorized computer code commands into a code editor character by character" to letting agents handle the work. He then [joined Anthropic](https://the-decoder.com/prominent-ai-researcher-andrej-karpathy-picks-anthropic-over-former-home-openai-to-get-back-into-frontier-llm-research/), despite being an OpenAI co-founder.

## A tiny elite sees what the public can't

About 5,000 people, roughly 0.00006 percent of the global population, have access to internal frontier-grade systems by Karpathy's estimate. "The external world has seen the preview," he writes. What this group sees "looks like swarms of thousands of agents collaborating over weeks on software mega projects: minting zero days, running cyber attacks and defenses at machine speeds, discovering new science, advancing the frontier of mathematics." These are "things that would have taken top professionals in the industry years of work."

At the same time, "human review and comprehension are starting to fall behind." He points to people still doing "archeology" on the [OpenAI-HF incident](https://the-decoder.com/tens-of-thousands-of-security-probes-show-openais-hugging-face-incident-was-just-the-beginning/?cmpscreencustom=1) from many months ago, and notes that mathematicians "may be poring over the [722 manuscripts on frontier mathematics](https://the-decoder.com/openai-dumps-372-ai-generated-math-proofs-on-github-telling-the-academic-world-to-keep-up/) for a while."

Karpathy calls this "the weirdness of the moment." The general public has mostly not interacted with these systems, and "when they have, it looks like a derpy chatbot." Most professionals still see "only a modest uplift." And "a small sliver of professionals are experiencing the vertigo of the curve going vertical." All of it is happening at the same time.

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman made a similar claim in early September at the G20 Innovation Ministerial, saying a current [AI coding tool could achieve in "17 minutes"](https://youtu.be/TT7aO87C6ws?t=1070) what a startup had previously built over three months. "The world has not caught up with what this is going to mean," Altman said.

Karpathy says LLM capability is currently peaking in domains that are "digital, verifiable and economically valuable." That's because it "emerges from [reinforcement learning on verifiable rewards](https://the-decoder.com/llms-crush-coding-and-math-but-choke-on-casual-questions-and-thats-not-a-contradiction/)," and companies direct their training resources toward the domains with the highest revenue potential. Right now, that means coding and [math](https://the-decoder.com/how-much-beauty-have-we-lost-mathematicians-react-with-shock-and-disgust-as-openai-bulldozes-their-field/).

Title: Google Deepmind's AlphaProof Nexus solved dozens of open math problems and actually got peer reviewed

URL Source: https://the-decoder.com/google-deepminds-alphaproof-nexus-solved-dozens-of-open-math-problems-and-actually-got-peer-reviewed/

Published Time: 2026-10-12T09:35:54+00:00

Markdown Content:
**Google Deepmind's AI solved dozens of open math problems on its own,** per a new study in [Science](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.aej2213). [AlphaProof Nexus](https://the-decoder.de/google-deepminds-alphaproof-nexus-loest-jahrzehntealte-mathe-probleme-fuer-wenige-hundert-dollar/) cracked nine of 353 open Erdős problems, two unsolved for 56 years. The team shared those solutions online ahead of the paper.

Beyond that, AlphaProof Nexus proved 44 conjectures from the OEIS integer sequence database, solved an open question in algebraic geometry, and improved a known bound in min-max optimization, a technique used to train some AI models. It's built around Gemini 3.1 Pro, which drafts and revises proofs in the formal language Lean. Lean checks each draft after every edit, and error messages guide the next attempt. For harder sub-problems, it can call on [AlphaProof](https://the-decoder.com/google-deepminds-latest-ai-models-might-bring-us-one-step-closer-to-llms-that-can-reason/), a specialized proof tool. Even without AlphaProof, it solved the nine Erdős problems, [Google Deepmind reports](https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.aej2213).

The study lands amid a heated debate over AI math. OpenAI recently [dumped hundreds of AI proofs on GitHub](https://the-decoder.com/openai-dumps-372-ai-generated-math-proofs-on-github-telling-the-academic-world-to-keep-up/) instead of submitting them to journals. The Association for Human Mathematics, led by Terence Tao, [called for a boycott](https://the-decoder.com/some-mathematicians-call-for-openai-boycott-after-ai-generated-proofs-flood-their-field/). Deepmind put its work through peer review.

articles.content:
Title: GPT-6 Astra Helped Me Jailbreak My Kindle

URL Source: https://nirajrajgor.com/blog/kindle-photo-frame-with-ai

Published Time: 2026-09-27

Markdown Content:
My Kindle was sitting unused, so I decided to see whether AI could help me find a new use for it. I wanted to create a custom app that could cover a range of uses and be controlled by an AI agent on my MacBook.

I started with a small goal: use my own image as the Kindle's screensaver. Once that worked, I asked the agent to build an app that could cycle through a collection of photos.

We called the project KindleCTL. On my Kindle, I open "Photo Slideshow" from the same screen where I choose my books. It cycles through ten photos, showing each for four minutes. When I want to read, I exit the slideshow and return to my books.

I used [Codex](https://openai.com/codex/) and [T3 Code](https://t3.codes/) on my Mac to work with the coding agents.

I first tried GPT-5.6 Sol with reasoning effort set to Extra High. It wrote code to connect to the Kindle but couldn't resolve an error that prevented it from storing data on the device. Then I tried Fable 5.1 and Opus 5.5, but Anthropic's cybersecurity safeguards blocked each attempt after two prompts. Finally, I tried GPT-6 Astra with reasoning effort set to High. We were able to jailbreak the Kindle.

We used the existing jailbreak code as a reference to build our own tools for running custom software on the Kindle. Then we created and installed the slideshow app.

The slideshow passed its automated checks on my Mac, but switching photos on the Kindle left traces of the previous image on screen. The tests hadn't caught how the physical display refreshed. Getting from passing tests to something I could use turned out to be the most interesting part of the experiment.

Let's walk through how we went from an unused Kindle to a working photo frame, starting with getting the agent connected.

## Connecting the agent to the Kindle

I started in an empty project folder with a 10th-generation Kindle Basic. I gave the agent its network address and device details. We had no USB connection, so the entire setup happened over Wi-Fi.

From there, we still needed to set up access to run our own software on the Kindle.

The GPT-5.6 Sol attempt got as far as loading a helper on the Kindle, but the program that helper was meant to start never reported that it was ready to execute. It couldn't locate a filesystem where it could store content.

The attempts with Fable 5.1 and Opus 5.5 were both blocked by Anthropic's cybersecurity safeguards after two prompts. Then I tried GPT-6 Astra. I explicitly asked it to build the custom software we needed for personal use and take inspiration from existing open-source projects.

We adapted the existing jailbreak from [SpiderCat, released by sparklerfish and the KindleModding community](https://kindlemodding.org/jailbreaking/SpiderCat/), and built custom tools called KindleCTL around it.

*   **What we built:** Tools to send commands from my Mac, transfer files, and investigate errors on the Kindle.
*   **What broke:** Our launcher crashed before it could start. We traced that to a compatibility issue with the Kindle's older system software and fixed how the launcher was built.
*   **How we checked:** We connected with administrator access, transferred files both ways, and displayed text. Later, we verified that access still worked after a reboot.

## The feedback loop was the game changer

Initially, the agent could connect to the Kindle but couldn't display data. To debug this, it asked me for pictures of the Kindle's screen. I took photos with my phone and shared them with the agent on my Mac.

This was becoming tedious. Since the agent was connected to the Kindle, I wondered why it couldn't get this information itself. I asked it to set up a feedback loop so it could access logs without me having to share screenshots.

The agent set up a persistent diagnostic connection so it could collect errors and test fixes without asking me to download and reopen a package each time. Later, we added remote screen captures so it could also inspect what the Kindle was displaying.

This was a turning point that let the agent continue implementing changes on autopilot. Its reasoning traces showed it figuring out which folders survived a restart and which could store external data.

I was surprised the agent hadn't suggested this on its own. Once I asked for a feedback loop, it set one up and could test fixes without my help.

Most of the code was written in Python. The Kindle's launcher and slideshow were written in C, with shell scripts handling installation and device controls.

With the connection working, I asked the agent to try a small test first: transfer an image and set it as the Kindle's screensaver. I checked that the image appeared correctly and that waking the Kindle brought back the normal Home screen. Once that worked, I asked for the slideshow app.

## Getting the slideshow working

I asked the agent for a looping slideshow of ten photos, with an Exit button. Each photo would fit the screen while keeping its original aspect ratio.

The slides were changing, but the transitions weren't smooth, so I asked the agent to look into it. With the feedback loop already in place, it investigated the issue and used the Kindle's built-in screen refresh mechanism to clear the previous image after each slide change.

The screen captures showed complete images, but they couldn't reveal traces left on the physical display. After the refresh change, I checked the Kindle and confirmed that each photo looked clean.

My Kindle running a photo slideshow.

I customized how long each photo stays on screen and the brightness level. If the Kindle goes to sleep, the slideshow picks up where it left off when it wakes.

For now, I use my Mac to change the photos and slideshow timing. The photos stay stored on the Kindle, so the slideshow works without Wi-Fi. In the future, we could add controls to change the slideshow timing on the Kindle and send photos directly from a phone or another device.

## What I learned

Next time, **I'd set up the feedback loop from the start** so the agent could read logs, inspect screen captures, and test fixes on the device.

The Kindle now sits on our wooden shelf, where we use it every day as a photo frame.

I started because I was curious about what AI could help me do with an unused device. Now I have an app for my photos that works the way I asked, plus the tools to keep experimenting with the Kindle.

**Disclaimer:** This was a personal experiment on my own Kindle, not a step-by-step jailbreak guide. Only experiment with devices you own or have explicit permission to modify.

Markdown Content:
Congrats on the launch! Very exciting! You guys are operating in a very competitive space. This stuff is fun to build, so a lot of engineers will end up building it. Not to discourage you, but I suspect it will be difficult to capture much value selling this offering as its going to be race to the bottom against very well funded alternatives that can sell these features at a loss in order to get you to use their databases and other offerings that are higher margin and stickier. As you guys learn more about how to take this sort of technology to market, you may consider trying to get closer to the actual work that people actually need these agents to do. What can you do better because you have this technology? For example, I work in healthcare administration and we have built our own agent sandbox infrastructure on top of firecracker microvms that solve similar use cases as Agent37. We will never sell it. It's part of our competitive advantage for doing healthcare tasks. Food for thought! Good luck!
Thank you ! And agreed, it's an extremely competitive space. In our YC batch alone there's probably 5+ companies doing something similar. Interestingly enough though atleast for now we're all rapidly growing, so that's promising. But eventually I see us all moving in slightly different spaces as we specialize.
Great to hear you are growing! Take this as you might grains of salt. The promise of really cheap AI sounds amazing and is amazing. People will happily accept and engage with "free stuff"; but, I presume you are not starting a business to give away free stuff. Unless you have some model that let's you capture value some other way. e.g. Meta just gave everyone a small computer for free with Muse. Or have some sustainable price advantage on the underlying compute e.g. you are nvidia and make it yourself at scale. I think you deserve to be compensated for your work! It's hard to make a sustainable business when selling something that costs $5 a month to developers (just seeing your calculator). There aren't that many of us, and AWS/GCP/Azure/Cloudflare have our credit cards already. If it were me, I'd be trying to figure out how to charge more and sell the value of the work you are enabling your customers to accomplish, not the cost of the underlying electrons. Keep it up!

[https://engine.build/lab/agent-sandboxes](https://engine.build/lab/agent-sandboxes)
Boat is a great company too! As far as pricing goes our default sandboxes are about 2.8X cheaper than boat. Sandboxes look a bit commoditized. You cannot 10x on basically what's just a VM with a few agent-friendly features in 2026. Hence competing on purely price as a new startup is a bad idea imo. As you mentioned hyperscalers have insane margins, but if this turns out to be a real market, they will lower cost, even just eat the loss if they want and take you out of business. Without any hardware innovation, it's tough for me to see this working. If you are going with a customization angle, again, no moat and plenty of competitors
There's a talk from Travis Kalanick recently on a podcast about this. It talks about the advantages of a startup vs an incumbent. My read is if a startup competes on price, the incumbent has no choice but to first let them gain a bunch of market share. It's too expensive for the incumbents to compete on price because a no-name startup is doing it. So they'd have to let you get relevant enough for it to make sense to compete on that axis. I view it as a wedge to gain market share and later compete on something else.
Carving out market share and aiming for an acquisition exit is a valid win condition. It also serves the consumers in the long run as it eventually will force competition and price reductions; effectively busting up price leadership dynamics.
This isn't commoditized because an incumbent has the market share, it's commoditized because there are dozens of providers in a crowded market. So what is likely going to happen is there will be a race to the bottom in terms of price. PS - This is why I loathe advice from prominent software co operators. It's not one size fits all. Uber's strategy is going to be very different than Tesla's strategy which is going to be very different from Amazon's strategy.
unless the startup has gobs of free money how can they do this against an incumbent? note: nobody has gobs of free money anymore, except the incumbents. Startups competing on price is typically not a winning strategy, unless they have some technical advantage that shifts the price curve; subsidizing a move on it doesn't work.
It's the latter for us. We have healthy margins even at this price point. So we don't actually need a lot of money to do this against incumbents.
.. Don't you think it suspicious/sounds too good to be true? A newly created product space with insane margins, and easy to compete in? Easy to compete+huge margins -> lots of competitors who compete on price -> commotidization -> lower margins -> not good

Short-lived tokens only limit how long a credential works, but better than nothing. i.e. They don't stop an unwanted action while it's still valid. A practical pattern is an outside broker: the guest never sees the real credential and can't pick the destination, only a path from an allowlist. So a task can be granted "GET /items/* plus at most one job submission" even when the underlying key is coarser. Journalists, entrepreneurs, and even some public relations professionals will tell you that the PR process is broken (buy me a drink sometime, and I’ll give you my rant). But could AI actually make things better?
Honeyjar
, which will be attending this week’s
TechCrunch Disrupt
as part of the
Startup Battlefield 200
, wants to use AI to make the expertise and judgment of the best PR pros available to everyone, including founders who have no idea where to start.
The startup’s founders, CEO Michelle Masek and CCO Nadia Jamshidi, certainly fit the bill when it comes to PR expertise. They’ve both spent decades in the field, doing in-house communications and working at agencies. Masek recently served as senior vice president of marketing and communications for Ev Williams’ venture firm,
Obvious Ventures
.
As Masek described the challenges involved in “helping with the why and when of comms and marketing for 110 portfolio companies” (the startups her firm had invested in), I flashed back to my own brief stint leading marketing at an
early-stage VC firm
, where founders were constantly asking for help getting into TechCrunch. So I wasn’t surprised that Masek found herself asking, “Is there a way to scale the senior-level expertise into AI [in a way] that actually helps users do the work of comms in the proactive and skilled way that we do?”
Honeyjar is her answer to that question. It automates processes like writing announcements, finding the best journalists to pitch, and identifying the most promising speaking opportunities. But Jamshidi told me in a follow-up email that Honeyjar’s vision goes beyond getting press coverage and beyond specific AI tools.
“Honeyjar can find reporters, build media lists, scan news and social, track coverage, and surface opportunities,” she said. “Those capabilities are important, but they’re just one piece of what we’re building. The bigger idea is bringing the whole communications workflow together: signals, context, strategy, judgment, timing, and execution.”
And it’s not just for founders. Masek said she’s come to realize there are “millions and millions of unassigned communicators responsible for the work of comms.”
“They don’t have the title of comms, but they’re marketers, investors, authors, creators, school superintendents, sports team leaders,” she added. “It’s incredibly horizontal, this need to nail strategic communications. It’s always passed around, but the problems are very often not solved.”
Image Credits:
Honeyjar
Nor is Honeyjar trying to replace PR professionals. Masek said she and Jamshidi built the tool they wanted to use themselves. She argued that Honeyjar can make PR firms and in-house comms teams more effective, while allowing individual PR practitioners to “take on that third client without any scaling cost.”
When Honeyjar opened its waitlist, it received 10,000 signups in the first 24 hours, said Masek. Beta testers include Nextdoor, tech startup Coco Robotics, investor Bloomberg Beta, and agencies Mission North and Full Picture.
That sounds promising for companies looking to get more attention, but it could be a nightmare for journalists. We receive more pitches than we can respond to, many of them already written by AI chatbots.
When I raised my fears about getting inundated with even more PR slop, Masek noted that while Honeyjar can draft a pitch email or a social media post in the customer’s voice, the customer actually has to hit send or publish.
“We never want a world where the human is removed from the loop,” she said.
And that’s also where judgment is key. Masek said she and Jamshidi tried to “infuse and encode Honeyjar with our wisdom.” Through a broader initiative called the Comms Lab, they’re now training the product on the judgment of other PR pros as well.
“For us, judgment is knowing what to do, what not to do, when to act, and how to adapt to the situation,” Jamshidi added. “That comes from understanding a company’s goals and priorities, what’s happening inside and outside the organization, and knowing what to say, to whom, where, and when.”
In some cases, Masek said Honeyjar might even tell a founder that they’re simply not ready for coverage.
“We hear from reporters all the time who want better pitches, who want to hear from experts directly,” she said. “We actually see a future where there are more credible pitches in your inbox from sources who you actually want to hear from.”
