Welcome to the second space race. You can be forgiven for experiencing déjà vu. Last time, it was the Soviet Union and the United States vying to be the first to plant some flags. Now it’s a sprint to the lunar surface between America and China—alongside a host of varyingly friendly and rival nations—plus a cornucopia of private spaceflight companies. And this time it looks like they’re getting ready to set up camp. There will be, the contenders say, bases on the moon, permanently inhabited castles under the stars.
The notion of a moon base, fanciful as it might sound, isn’t new. But this year, under the leadership of Administrator Jared Isaacman, NASA has been flooding the zone with
bold announcements
. If all goes according to plan—a plan that will likely cost tens of billions of dollars to start—there will be
drones
, robotic landers,
communication satellites
, and a
nuclear power plant
; there will be plant terrariums and moonquake sensors; there will be mechanized scouts exploring craters for water.
Initial astronaut missions to the lunar surface, which the US is currently planning to start in 2028, will be focused on exploration and technological experimentation. But the idea is that we will—some time in the 2030s—get to a point where there will be habitation quarters for long-term stays, surrounded by a network of scientific research stations, resource mining and processing plants, and landing pads for spaceships. “It’s going to be an expanse,” says Carlos García-Galán, NASA’s moon base program manager—one that will add up to “hundreds of square miles.”
The effort is undoubtedly being fueled by nationalistic competition. China has near-identical plans to build its own base on the moon. And being first matters, because the “victor” gets to define the terms. What
is
the moon, exactly? Is it a militarized outpost? Is it a manufacturing hub? Is it a wilderness to be studied and preserved?
But there are also other reasons to go. Earth’s companion contains
primeval rocks
that hold clues to the formation of the entire solar system. The lunar surface, with virtually no atmosphere in the way, is an ideal place to put telescopes that could examine the most
ancient epochs
of the cosmos. The far side of the moon would be “a fantastic place to explore the further universe,” says Josef Aschbacher, the European Space Agency’s director general. And it’s way more energy efficient to launch rockets from the low-gravity lunar surface than it is from Earth, meaning sending astronauts—or robotic spacecraft—farther into the solar system will become much less difficult. “The moon is critical. It will be a stepping stone for going further—that means to Mars and beyond,” says Aschbacher.
SELMAN DESIGN
But if these bold visions are to become reality, there’s a daunting amount of work to be done. A sprawling moon base must be safe for its astronaut inhabitants—protected from falling asteroids, endless cosmic radiation, razor-sharp lunar dust, and torturous temperature swings. It also must be somewhat self-sustaining, so that it can weather changing political fortunes and not cost ruinous amounts of money to maintain. For that, we’ll need to find a way to use the moon’s resources to keep the base operating—and ideally generating revenue. And we’ll need autonomous robots that can build, maintain, and expand the base even when their human masters aren’t present. “It’s almost like starting civilization from scratch,” says Simon Middleburgh, co-director of the Nuclear Futures Institute at Bangor University in Wales.
Assuming we can overcome these starting challenges, decades from now—let’s say, by the year 2100—our initial moon bases could grow from barely visible structures into luminous cities, perhaps not too dissimilar from those dreamed up by authors and screenwriters the world over. “It’s like science fiction today that we really want to turn into a reality,” says García-Galán. Will anyone succeed?
The moon is a tremendously hostile place to set up camp. In general, daytime temperatures can reach more than 250 °F; at night, they can plummet to less than –200 °F. Exposed to the vacuum of space, the surface is constantly showered in carcinogenic radiation and frequently hit by meteoroids. And its volcanic dust is sticky and corrosive, a destroyer of equipment and choker of lungs.
Sadly, the lunar south pole—the area NASA is targeting—is even harsher. NASA wants to build a base there because its permanently shadowed craters are thought to harbor caches of water ice, which would be more precious than gold. Purify it, and you can water crops and hydrate astronauts; split it into oxygen and hydrogen, and you have breathable air and rocket propellant. But the temperature in those craters can be lower than –410 °F, making them some of the coldest places in the known universe. On the surface outside those pits, astronauts would be bathed in the scorching sun for 14 days before experiencing an equally long frigid night.
But there is only so much money we can spend on safety. “What it comes down to is acceptable risk of death,”
Philip Metzger
, a spaceflight engineering researcher at the Florida Space Institute, said while pondering some of the dangers. “What can we reasonably survive without breaking the bank?”
Temperature is one of the easiest problems to handle. Materials science has come a long way, and there are myriad metals, ceramics, plastics, compounds, and alloys that can resist wild temperature swings. Radiators keep things cool; heaters keep batteries from dying prematurely. Astronauts survive just fine too, with their fancy spacesuits—but that technology has proved itself only during brief excursions. It’s not yet clear how long this equipment could operate under such tempestuous conditions.
The temperature in the moon’s south pole craters can be lower than –410 °F, making them some of the coldest places in the known universe.
Outside those pits, astronauts would be bathed in the scorching sun for 14 days before experiencing an equally long frigid night.
Space radiation, which can wreak havoc on electronics and trigger a cancerous division of cells, is far more pernicious. And as Stuart George, a physicist at NASA’s Johnson Space Center in Houston, explains, it comes in two unpleasant forms.
The first is
galactic cosmic rays
, which rain down on the moon almost constantly. “They’re made by supernovas and neutron star mergers—all these kinds of things,” says George. And because the atomic nuclei, protons, and electrons that make them up are moving at significant fractions of the speed of light, these cosmic rays have oodles of kinetic energy, meaning they can punch through thin shielding (say, a metal wall) with ease. “They also have this habit where the heavier ions are fragmenting in that shielding and making secondary particles,” says George. That means if your shield is too thin, the astronauts behind it will be blasted with a surprisingly large dose of radiation.
Then you have the sun. It may sustain life on Earth, but without our planet’s thick atmosphere and magnetic bubble to get in its way, moonwalkers will occasionally be blasted by one of its paroxysms: a solar flare (a burst of diverse types of radiation) or a coronal mass ejection (volleys of magnetized plasma). “During Apollo, they knew that if a large solar flare occurred while the crew was on the moon, there would be no way to keep them alive,” says Metzger. The crew could have developed acute radiation sickness and perished in a matter of days.
The way to survive a powerful solar flare or coronal mass ejection is straightforward: “Get back inside a habitat where there’s more shielding,” says George—preferably a dedicated, highly shielded “storm shelter,” essentially a thick-walled bunker. The issue is that astronauts might be outside the base, driving a rover many miles away. Coronal mass ejections take hours to days to reach the vicinity of the Earth-moon system, but solar flares can do so in under an hour. And scientists can’t yet model the sun well enough to give much advance notice. “All of the capability to forecast solar storms is kind of like where weather forecasting [was] … in the ’50s and ’60s,” says George.
As for those punchy galactic cosmic rays, the only way to avoid them would be to put a
lot
of stuff—lunar rocks, possibly—between the astronauts and the sky. “Build habitat modules underground,” says
Chris Dreyer
, director of engineering at the Center for Space Resources at the Colorado School of Mines. One option: Burrow living quarters into lava tubes, the naturally hollowed-­out volcanic tunnels created by molten rock eons ago. At this point, NASA hasn’t mentioned any plans to make its moon base subterranean, but it may need to if it wants to end up with a small lunar city.
Radiation limits the time astronauts can spend on the lunar surface over their entire life—it can total around two years max, experts estimate, before the health risk becomes too high. Unfortunately, that’s not all space will throw at them. When the Artemis II astronauts swung around the far side of the moon earlier this year, they saw
curious flashes
light up the silvery land below. These were the explosive deaths of small meteoroids punching into the lunar surface.
Earth is naturally protected from smaller space rocks, up to around 50 feet in diameter: They burn up inconsequentially in the atmosphere. “You don’t have that option on the moon,” says
Philip Lubin
, a physicist and planetary defense researcher at the University of California, Santa Barbara. Since smaller rocks plunge toward planets and moons far more frequently than larger ones do, this means the moon is often peppered by what are effectively tiny space bullets. They could easily puncture a spacesuit or the engine of a moon rover.
How do you protect astronauts from the onslaught? “The simplest answer is burial,” says
Nicholas Schmerr
, a planetary seismologist at the University of Maryland—conveniently, the same way you’d deal with radiation exposure. Pile up moon rocks onto your base walls or put habitable structures in lava tubes.
Inconveniently, there’s always a chance that a bigger asteroid will come along. Even buried habitation modules would have trouble surviving an assault from a 50-footer—about the length of a semi-trailer.
That doesn’t mean a moon base would be helpless against bigger asteroids. Planetary defense has come a long way in just a few decades. NASA’s DART mission demonstrated that it could deflect an asteroid by
ramming into the rock
with an uncrewed spacecraft, and cutting-­edge experiments at clandestine labs around the US suggest that a nuclear bomb could swat away or
entirely vaporize
errant space rocks. An array of both ground-based and space-based telescopes specifically designed to
spy killers
—such as the ATLAS quartet of largely automated telescopes, and the soon-to-be-launched NEO Surveyor infrared telescope—are also aiming to find 90% of the near-Earth asteroids potentially capable of wiping out entire cities (those 460 feet across) in the coming years.
All these protections apply to the moon. But asteroids 50 feet across are so stealthy that even NASA’s best telescopes would struggle to see them years or even months in advance. Odds are that they would first be seen not long before they were due to hit the lunar surface. Then what?
It’s not unreasonable to imagine several turret-like launch sites on the moon that, owing to the lower gravity and airless environment, could rapidly fire projectiles toward an incoming asteroid. Hit it hard enough and it would break into fragments. Just make sure you shoot when it is as far away as possible: “If you were to break something up into a thousand pieces, then you have a thousand impacts on the moon,” says Lubin. “That might be worse than letting it hit one place.”

Title: Clearing chat history helps AI agents find better solutions

URL Source: https://the-decoder.com/clearing-chat-history-helps-ai-agents-find-better-solutions/

Published Time: 2026-10-12T16:10:00+00:00

Markdown Content:
Oct 12, 2026

Nano Banana Pro prompted by THE DECODER

*   [Clearing chat history lets agents explore new approaches](https://the-decoder.com/clearing-chat-history-helps-ai-agents-find-better-solutions/#clearing-chat-history-lets-agents-explore-new-approaches)
*   [A 66 percent higher normalized average score on the same compute budget](https://the-decoder.com/clearing-chat-history-helps-ai-agents-find-better-solutions/#a-66-percent-higher-normalized-average-score-on-the-same-compute-budget)
*   [Stronger models may still need context resets](https://the-decoder.com/clearing-chat-history-helps-ai-agents-find-better-solutions/#stronger-models-may-still-need-context-resets)

**Long-running AI research agents can plateau despite additional compute, a Microsoft Research study finds. Accumulated conversation context can constrain their search, keeping them focused on similar solutions instead of exploring better approaches.**

Microsoft researchers studied what they call "Autoresearch agents," AI systems that repeatedly propose solutions, evaluate them, and refine them based on feedback. Eight independent runs of the same agent on the same task plateaued at significantly different performance levels, with final scores ranging from 68.3 to 100.0. These gaps persisted even with substantially more compute, according to the paper.

## Agents get stuck in "idea basins"

[The researchers plotted](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.07447) solutions from all runs on a two-dimensional map that places similar solutions close together, then compared them. Solutions from a single run almost always stayed within a small region of the map. The authors call these regions "idea basins."

The agents spend a large share of their remaining compute budget refining solutions within a less productive region instead of finding better approaches discovered by other runs. This pattern persists even when the agents periodically compress their conversation histories.

## Clearing chat history lets agents explore new approaches

The proposed method, "Fork-and-Flush," combines two mechanisms. In "forking," the agent splits into K parallel branches, each inheriting the previous workspace and all generated files. In "flushing," each branch loses its entire chat context but keeps the workspace, allowing it to start a fresh conversation and build on prior work.

On the left, a single run (gray, dashed) keeps refining solutions within the same idea basin. Fork-and-Flush starts parallel branches with fresh chat contexts, keeps the best branch, and discards the rest. On the right, a branch with fresh context moves into a different idea basin and achieves a higher score. | Image: Cai, Ziakas et al. (2026)

A branch that keeps the parent process's chat context tends to return to the same idea basin because the previous reasoning steers its next steps. Fresh context restores diversity in the search. The conversation history is lost, but the code, files, and saved results remain in the workspace.

## A 66 percent higher normalized average score on the same compute budget

The researchers tested Fork-and-Flush on [13 long-running tasks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07447), including polyomino packing, job-shop scheduling, and cryptanalysis. The tasks also included compressing a CIFAR classifier and optimizing a VLIW kernel. Individual runs lasted from several hours to over 100 hours. The agents used GPT-5.6-terra and GPT-5.5 through the GitHub Copilot CLI.

On the same compute budget, Fork-and-Flush achieved a min-max-normalized average score of 0.78, compared to 0.47 for single runs and 0.54 for best-of-4. The paper reports relative gains of 66.0 and 44.4 percent, respectively. The method achieved the highest mean score on 12 of the 13 tasks.

Fork-and-Flush also produced more consistent results, with normalized standard deviation falling to 0.16 from 0.26 for single runs. Simply clearing the chat context without branching improved results by 22 percent.

| Evaluation | Method | Normalized Average Score | Normalized Standard Deviation | Relative improvement over the respective single-run baseline |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 13 tasks | Single run | 0.47 | 0.26 | Baseline |
| 13 tasks | Best-of-4 | 0.54 | 0.21 | approx. +14.9% |
| 13 tasks | Fork-and-Flush | 0.78 | 0.16 | +66.0% |
| 11 tasks | Single run | 0.45 | — | Baseline |
| 11 tasks | Flushing only | 0.55 | — | approx. +22% |

## Stronger models may still need context resets

The researchers also tested whether more capable models avoid idea basins, using [MAX-3-SAT problems](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MAX-3SAT) across three model sizes, Qwen3.5-4B, 9B, and 27B. Variance between runs followed an inverted U-shaped curve, peaking on tasks at the edge of a model's abilities, roughly halfway between random-guessing performance and the reference solver's performance.

Results vary most on tasks at the edge of a model's abilities, with some runs succeeding and others falling well short. Models almost always succeed on very easy tasks and fail on very hard ones. This pattern holds across all three model sizes tested. | Image: Cai, Ziakas et al. (2026)

The authors argue that open research problems sit, by definition, at the limits of models' abilities. They expect the variation Fork-and-Flush exploits to persist as models improve, with the boundary simply shifting toward harder problems. The results suggest that regular context resets could remain useful even for frontier research agents.

Title: Kevin Kelly's 2016 AI Predictions, 10 Years Later

URL Source: https://taylor.town/kk-ai-2026

Published Time: 2026-10-12T00:00:00.000Z

Markdown Content:
[Kevin Kelly](https://kk.org/)'s [_The Inevitable_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Inevitable_%28book%29) articulates a handful of macro technological trends and follows them to their logical conclusions. It's an insightful read -- I highly recommend it.

One decade later, here are some AI-related excerpts from the book:

*   ["By 2026, Google’s main product will not be search but AI."](https://taylor.town/kk-ai-2026#1)
*   ["oligarchy of two or three large, general-purpose cloud-based commercial intelligences"](https://taylor.town/kk-ai-2026#2)
*   ["The AI on the horizon looks more like Amazon Web Services"](https://taylor.town/kk-ai-2026#3)
*   ["The bulk of AI will be special purpose software brains"](https://taylor.town/kk-ai-2026#4)
*   ["in conversational tones, any question at all"](https://taylor.town/kk-ai-2026#5)

## "By 2026, Google’s main product will not be search but AI."

> Around 2002 I attended a private party for Google—before its IPO, when it was a small company focused only on search. I struck up a conversation with Larry Page, Google’s brilliant cofounder. “Larry, I still don’t get it. There are so many search companies. Web search, for free? Where does that get you?” My unimaginative blindness is solid evidence that predicting is hard, especially about the future, but in my defense this was before Google had ramped up its ad auction scheme to generate real income, long before YouTube or any other major acquisitions. I was not the only avid user of its search site who thought it would not last long. But Page’s reply has always stuck with me: “Oh, we’re really making an AI.”
>
>
> I’ve thought a lot about that conversation over the past few years as Google has bought 13 other AI and robotics companies in addition to DeepMind. At first glance, you might think that Google is beefing up its AI portfolio to improve its search capabilities, since search constitutes 80 percent of its revenue. But I think that’s backward. Rather than use AI to make its search better, Google is using search to make its AI better. Every time you type a query, click on a search-generated link, or create a link on the web, you are training the Google AI. When you type “Easter Bunny” into the image search bar and then click on the most Easter Bunny–looking image, you are teaching the AI what an Easter Bunny looks like. Each of the 3 billion queries that Google conducts each day tutors the deep-learning AI over and over again. With another 10 years of steady improvements to its AI algorithms, plus a thousandfold more data and a hundred times more computing resources, Google will have an unrivaled AI. In a quarterly earnings conference call in the fall of 2015, Google CEO Sundar Pichai stated that AI was going to be “a core transformative way by which we are rethinking everything we are doing. . . . We are applying it across all our products, be it search, be it YouTube and Play, etc.” My prediction: By 2026, Google’s main product will not be search but AI.

In 2017, Google researchers published [_Attention Is All You Need_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Attention_Is_All_You_Need), which introduced a deep-learning architecture called the _transformer_.

## "oligarchy of two or three large, general-purpose cloud-based commercial intelligences"

> As it does, this cloud-based AI will become an increasingly ingrained part of our everyday life. But it will come at a price. Cloud computing empowers the law of increasing returns, sometimes called the network effect, which holds that the value of a network increases much faster as it grows bigger. The bigger the network, the more attractive it is to new users, which makes it even bigger and thus more attractive, and so on. A cloud that serves AI will obey the same law. The more people who use an AI, the smarter it gets. The smarter it gets, the more people who use it. The more people who use it, the smarter it gets. And so on. Once a company enters this virtuous cycle, it tends to grow so big so fast that it overwhelms any upstart competitors. As a result, our AI future is likely to be ruled by an oligarchy of two or three large, general-purpose cloud-based commercial intelligences.

Kelly predicted AI heavyweights while advocating for a future of open weights:

> Ideally, this additional intelligence should be not just cheap, but free. A free AI, like the free commons of the web, would feed commerce and science like no other force we can imagine and would pay for itself in no time.

## "The AI on the horizon looks more like Amazon Web Services"

> Amid all this activity, a picture of our AI future is coming into view, and it is not the HAL 9000—a discrete machine animated by a charismatic (yet potentially homicidal) humanlike consciousness—or a Singularitan rapture of superintelligence. The AI on the horizon looks more like Amazon Web Services—cheap, reliable, industrial-grade digital smartness running behind everything, and almost invisible except when it blinks off. This common utility will serve you as much IQ as you want but no more than you need. You’ll simply plug into the grid and get AI as if it was electricity.

## "The bulk of AI will be special purpose software brains"

Not even Kelly foresaw [the bitter lesson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bitter_lesson):

> Yet most of the commercial work completed by AI will be done by nonhuman-like programs. The bulk of AI will be special purpose software brains that can, for example, translate any language into any other language, but do little else. Drive a car, but not converse. Or recall every pixel of every video on YouTube, but not anticipate your work routines. In the next 10 years, 99 percent of the artificial intelligence that you will interact with, directly or indirectly, will be nerdly narrow, supersmart specialists.

## "in conversational tones, any question at all"

> Very soon now we’ll live in a world where we can ask the cloud, in conversational tones, any question at all. And if that question has a known answer, the machine will explain it to us. Who won the Rookie of the Year Award in 1974? Why is the sky blue? Will the universe keep expanding forever? Over time the cloud, or Cloud, the machine, or AI, will learn to articulate what is known and not known. At first it may need to engage us in a dialog to clarify ambiguities (as we humans do when answering questions), but, unlike us, the answer machine will not hesitate to provide deep, obscure, complex factual knowledge on any subject—if it exists.
>
>
> …
>
>
> As we cognify more books and movies and the internet of things, answers become ubiquitous. We are headed to a future where we will ask several hundred questions per day. Most of these questions will concern us and our friends. “Where is Jenny? What time is the next bus? Is this kind of snack good?” The “manufacturing costs” of each answer will be nanocents. Search, as in “give me an answer,” will no longer be considered a first-world luxury. It will become an essential universal commodity.

# AI coding agents generate more code, but not more software

Study finds coding efficiency gains get “absorbed” by human review “bottleneck.”

[Kyle Orland](https://arstechnica.com/author/kyle-orland/) – Oct 9, 2026 7:43 PM|[283](https://arstechnica.com/ai/2026/10/ai-coding-agents-generate-more-code-but-not-more-software/#comments "283 comments")

Anyone who has even tangentially associated with computer programming knows that modern AI coding assistants and agents [can be incredibly efficient at generating huge amounts of functional code](https://arstechnica.com/ai/2026/01/developers-say-ai-coding-tools-work-and-thats-precisely-what-worries-them/). But coders making use of those tools also [know better than to trust the accuracy of that code](https://arstechnica.com/ai/2025/07/developer-survey-shows-trust-in-ai-coding-tools-is-falling-as-usage-rises/), meaning [substantial effort needs to be spent](https://arstechnica.com/ai/2025/05/time-saved-by-ai-offset-by-new-work-created-study-suggests/) reviewing any AI-generated output.

[A recent study](https://fion.ac/jellyfish.pdf) of actual coding practices across hundreds of firms finds that human code review forms a significant “bottleneck” for the overall efficiency of AI coding tools, resulting in “little evidence that firms increase software output or reduce employment” by using them. Any efficiency increased during the actual coding phase, the study authors find, is “absorbed by downstream constraints in the production process”; as “the code review process significantly increases in length, pull requests are more likely to require revisions, and reviewers leave more comments.”

## Cut once, measure twice

To come to these conclusions, Harvard University researchers Fiona Chen and James Stratton made use of aggregated analytics data from [Jellyfish](https://jellyfish.co/), which measures the granular output of engineering teams. That data encompasses 300 million individual “work events” (e.g., commits and pull requests) and issue management software data across more than 700,000 employees at over 700 relevant software development firms from 2021 through March of 2026.

To assess the impact of AI tools on these firms, the researchers used a mix of directly measured AI usage and analyses of GitHub activity to determine when each company started introducing either AI coding assistants (which can help auto-complete code primarily authored by humans) and/or AI coding agents (which primarily write and submit code autonomously based on prompts) into their workflows. The researchers then perform some complicated math to determine a “difference of differences” regression on key variables both before and after the introduction of these tools at different points in time across different organizations.

 If there’s one thing AI coding agents are good at, it’s churning out a lot of code.

 Credit: [Chen and Stratton](https://fion.ac/jellyfish.pdf)

 If there’s one thing AI coding agents are good at, it’s churning out a lot of code.  Credit: [Chen and Stratton](https://fion.ac/jellyfish.pdf)

### Ars Video

### [How The Callisto Protocol's Gameplay Was Perfected Months Before Release](https://www.arstechnica.com/video/watch/how-the-callisto-protocols-gameplay-was-perfected-months-before-release)

In terms of raw code being produced, the results are clear and stark. The introduction of AI coding agents at a firm leads to a 30 percent increase in total lines of code generated, a 20 percent rise in the number of total commits, and a 23 percent increase in pull requests on average, the researchers write. But all that extra code doesn’t translate directly into improved software output on the firm level. On the contrary, the resolution rate for Issues and Epics (i.e. wholesale software features) tracked by tools like Jira did not change in a statistically significant way after AI tools were introduced (the researchers also found no “compositional shift” in the size or complexity of those Jira-tracked issues across the AI introduction).

The reason for that discrepancy can be found directly in the code review process, which takes markedly longer on average after the introduction of AI coding agents. Overall, the average “review process” time between a pull request getting submitted and it being merged into the codebase balloons 49 percent on average after AI agents are introduced. That effect can be seen in more granular data, too, with “the share of pull requests with changes requested nearly doubl[ing], and the number of comments per pull request increas[ing] by 35%” following the AI agent shift, the researchers write.

In response to this change, the researchers found a 14 percent increase in the share of workers performing code reviews after AI agents’ introduction. They also write that they “cannot attribute significant employment changes to AI” after looking at total active workers across Jellyfish and cross-referencing with LinkedIn data at those firms.

 Pull requests need changes a lot more often in the “agentic coding” era.

 Credit: [Chen and Stratton](https://fion.ac/jellyfish.pdf)

 Pull requests need changes a lot more often in the “agentic coding” era.  Credit: [Chen and Stratton](https://fion.ac/jellyfish.pdf)

While AI could also theoretically help with this review process, the researchers found that, so far, that impact has been marginal. Although 80 percent of measured firms used some form of AI code review by March 2026, AI agents were only responsible for 23.3 percent of all review comments and 10.8 percent of all pull requests, suggesting humans were still responsible for the vast majority of this work.

AI agents are still a relatively new part of the coding world, of course, and there have been significant updates and upgrades to their output even since this study’s March 2026 data cutoff. And while 95 percent of firms in the study have implemented AI coding agents by this point, many are doubtlessly still going through a learning process regarding when and how to best deploy them. These kinds of “coding time versus review time” trade-offs could improve as software engineering teams gain more experience with the pros and cons of siccing an AI agent on particular coding problems.

For now, though, letting AI write your code looks like a double-edged sword, with increases in coding speed counteracted by similar increases in human code review time and effort. It’s the kind of result that makes us wonder if the considerable time and expense to get AI coding agents working is really worth it for most companies.

**37 tok/s from Qwen3-Next-80B (a 48 GB model) on a laptop with 32 GB of memory, 24 without drafts, where llama.cpp manages 2.8; reading a prompt, 62 tok/s against 16.** Janas-LLM was faster than llama.cpp on every model compared on the same laptop (Debian 13 Linux, Intel Core Ultra 9 185H, its integrated Arc GPU, 32 GB, an NVMe SSD; 9-11 October 2026; the whole machine [below](https://github.com/prabanta-dev/janas#the-machine-it-grew-on)):

| Model | reading 1,024 tokens: Janas-LLM | llama.cpp | writing: Janas-LLM | llama.cpp |

One exception: the 3-bit Qwen3-30B reads a prompt slower than llama.cpp, since its Q3_K weights do not go to the GPU's fast prompt yet; it writes three times as fast.

How they were measured, and the speeds with the drafts: [What works now](https://github.com/prabanta-dev/janas#what-works-now). On another machine the figures will be other ones: `janas-bench` measures yours.

**Try it** on Linux x86-64 (Ubuntu 22.04, Debian 12 and later):

curl -LO https://github.com/prabanta-dev/janas/releases/latest/download/janas-linux-x86_64.tar.gz
tar xf janas-linux-x86_64.tar.gz && cd janas
./janas-chat                     # the models it knows: pick one, it is downloaded and checked

**Or on Windows** 10 (1903 or later) and 11, x86-64: download [janas-windows-x86_64.zip](https://github.com/prabanta-dev/janas/releases/latest/download/janas-windows-x86_64.zip), unpack it, and in a terminal in its `janas` folder run `.\janas-chat`. On the same laptop under Windows 11 (12 October 2026) Janas-LLM wrote as fast as on Linux (Qwen3-4B 25.6 tok/s, Qwen3-30B-A3B 34.2) and read a prompt as fast with the mixture (Qwen3-30B-A3B 132 tok/s) and 1.8 times as fast with the dense model (Qwen3-4B 346 tok/s against 193), whose whole blocks go to the GPU, through Intel's own Windows driver there.

The models come already converted from [Hugging Face](https://huggingface.co/prabanta-dev); building from the sources: [Getting started](https://github.com/prabanta-dev/janas#getting-started).

```
▄███████████▄
▄███████████████▄
███ ▄ █████ ▄ ███ ▄   J A N A S
███▄▄▄█████▄▄▄████
▀█████▄▀▀▀▄█████▀ ▀   a family of tools for artificial intelligence, in C
  █████████████
 █ █ █ █ █ █ █ █
▀ ▀ ▀ ▀ ▀ ▀ ▀ ▀
```

Janas is a family of tools for artificial intelligence, written in C with no dependencies beyond the C library. Its first component, **Janas-LLM**, runs large mixture-of-experts language models on ordinary computers, with or without a GPU: the weights stay on disk, the experts each token needs are streamed from an NVMe SSD, and the ones that keep coming back stay in memory. An 80-billion parameter model runs, and answers, on a laptop with 32 GB of RAM.

Designed and written by **Maurizio "camauri" Cammalleri**.

* * *

## ⚠️ Read this first

**This is an experiment, not a product.**

|  |  |
| --- | --- |
| **Stage** | Early development. The public API and the command line **change without notice**, and have changed several times a week. The models' files are the exception: the `.jns` files published on Hugging Face (format version 2) will be read by every later version of Janas-LLM. |
| **Stability** | **Not verified.** The engine is deliberately hard on the machine: it fills the free memory with its expert cache and reads the disk at full speed with `O_DIRECT`. On a machine with less headroom than it reckons, the desktop can be pushed into swap and become slow or unresponsive. Using a GPU has, once, caused a driver reset that took the desktop with it. |
| **Data** | It writes only in `~/.cache/janas` (what it learns about your machine, and the system messages it has read, so as not to read them again) and where you tell it to put a converted model. It does not touch the model files it reads. |
| **Hardware** | Developed and run on **one** machine (below). On anything else it is untested: it may be slower, it may refuse the model, it may misbehave. |

If something goes wrong, `Ctrl-C` stops a reply and `Ctrl-D` leaves the chat; `--cache <GiB>` puts a hard limit on the memory it takes, and `JANAS_GPU=0` keeps it off the GPU entirely.

## The machine it grew on

Everything in this repository was written and measured on:

*   **Linux Debian 13** (trixie), x86-64, kernel 6.12.107; GPU driver Mesa 26.1.6 (Vulkan); built with GCC 14.2
*   **Intel Core Ultra 9 185H** (6 performance cores, 8 efficiency, 2 low-power; AVX2, FMA, F16C, AVX-VNNI; integrated Arc GPU)
*   **32 GB** of DDR5 RAM
*   **1 TB NVMe SSD** (about 5.7 GB/s reading)

The Windows build was run on the same laptop under Windows 11 (build 26300), with Intel's own graphics driver: its tests pass there, and how fast it was is under **Or on Windows**, above.

Everything the engine does is chosen from what it measures, so another machine will make other choices — that part is meant to travel. What has never been tried is the rest: other CPUs (especially without AVX-VNNI, or AMD), discrete GPUs, slower disks, more or less memory. **If you run it somewhere else, the report from `janas-bench` is the single most useful thing you can send back** (see [Helping it run on more hardware](https://github.com/prabanta-dev/janas/blob/main/docs/hardware.md#helping-it-run-on-more-hardware)).

## What works now

What Janas-LLM runs today, model by model and feature by feature: [docs/features.md](https://github.com/prabanta-dev/janas/blob/main/docs/features.md).

On the machine above, with nothing else running, `janas-bench` reports this (measured on 10 October 2026, with the fast prompt the engine uses by default since that day):

| Model | reading a prompt | writing a reply | with drafts, in a chat |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Qwen3.5-2B (dense, 1.3 GB) | 395 tok/s | 50 tok/s | **67 tok/s** |
| Qwen3-4B (dense, 2.5 GB) | 220 tok/s | 28 tok/s | see `--draft` below |
| Qwen3.5-9B (dense, 5.7 GB) | 103 tok/s | 14 tok/s | **24 tok/s** |
| Qwen3-30B-A3B (18.6 GB) | 133 tok/s | 34 tok/s | — |
| Qwen3.6-35B-A3B (22.3 GB) | 86 tok/s | 25 tok/s | **34 tok/s** |
| Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B (48.4 GB) | 64 tok/s | 22 tok/s | **37 tok/s** |
| Gemma-4-E2B-it (3.1 GB) | 211 tok/s | 38 tok/s | **52 tok/s** |
| Gemma-4-E4B-it (5.0 GB) | 133 tok/s | 20 tok/s | **32 tok/s** |
| Gemma-4-12B-it (dense, 7.1 GB) | 71 tok/s | 10 tok/s | **14 tok/s** |
| Gemma-4-26B-A4B-it (18.3 GB) | 90 tok/s | 18 tok/s | **26 tok/s** |

Every figure is the **mean of three rounds**, not a best round, of the configuration the engine itself chose for each kind of pass - the one a chat runs: a prompt of 256 tokens, then 64 written. Here the integrated GPU reads every prompt (the fast prompt, below), and the threads the engine settled on were the performance cores' 12 for a prompt and for a single token on nearly every model, all the usable cores (performance and efficiency, not the low-power ones) for a few tokens at once. On another machine the engine may settle on other threads: the first passes of each kind try every core, one thread per performance core and the performance cores' threads, keep the fastest, and later try the others now and then, so that a machine that warms up can change the verdict (on an i9-14900HX every thread replied at less than half the speed of the performance cores' 16). The rounds run in alternating order so that the machine warming up and the cache filling weigh on each setting alike. Expect a few per cent either way between runs, and rather less than these on a first run, while the cache is still filling. Without the GPU (`JANAS_GPU=0`) Qwen3-4B reads the same prompt at 85 tok/s and writes at 27.

The last column is a draft guessing the next tokens and the model checking them, which is the same text at a higher rate — the whole of it is explained under [`--mtp`](https://github.com/prabanta-dev/janas/blob/main/docs/chat.md): the Qwen3.5 and Qwen3.6 models' and Qwen3-Next's own prediction block, Gemma 4's assistant (a small drafting model of its own). It is measured on a chat reply: an ordinary question in English ("explain how bread is made at home"), 64 tokens of the answer, sampled as the chat samples. **What the draft is worth depends on the text**: there the drafts survived 74-89% of the time on the Qwen models and Gemma's two larger ones, 63-72% on Gemma's E2B and E4B; on Italian prose Qwen3.5-2B kept about a third of them, and gained next to nothing. One round of 64 tokens is noisy here, a tenth either way between runs. Qwen3-30B-A3B has no such block, nor have the dense Qwen3; the dense Qwen3.5 have one in their original checkpoint, which `hf2jns_mtp` converts ([MODELS.md](https://github.com/prabanta-dev/janas/blob/main/MODELS.md#the-fingerprints)).

**This column was wrong until 26 September 2026**, and higher: it measured the block continuing a paragraph that repeated itself, which a model copies and the block guesses almost every time - 107 tok/s for Qwen3.5-2B, 26 for Qwen3.5-9B. The MoE figures of the time (29 and 30) happened to be lower than today's; the ChangeLog has the details.

The comparison with llama.cpp at the top of this page was measured so: llama.cpp (build `2b18470` of 18 September 2026) with its Vulkan backend on the same integrated GPU, everything on it (`llama-bench -p 1024 -n 16 -ngl 99 -t 12`; the largest model otherwise, below), against `janas-bench --prompt 1024 --gen 16` on the same files the same days (9-11 October 2026; llama.cpp's best configuration, Janas-LLM's own choice; on 11 October three rounds each, `llama-bench -r 3` and `janas-bench --rounds 3`, for Qwen3-0.6B, Qwen3.5-0.8B, Qwen3.6-35B-A3B and the models from other hands; Qwen3-Coder-Next as Qwen3-Next-80B, below).

On Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B, whose file is larger than this laptop's 30 GB, llama.cpp with its usual build ran out of memory as soon as the GPU took part, even with the experts left on the CPU (`-ngl 99 -ncmoe 48`): its CPU backend copies the weights into memory of its own to repack them, and the Vulkan backend copies those it leaves to the CPU into buffers the system cannot reclaim. articles.content:
In a research station in central Panama, you can walk through a century of forest time, watching scrubby plots of adolescent trees give way to cathedral-­like canopies of mature growth. Forest ecologist Daisy Dent, a senior scientist at ETH Zurich, oversees this sequence of plots across the Barro Colorado Nature Monument, some of which date as far back as the 19th century. Not one of the trees she surveys was planted by human hands. She maps, measures, and tracks each trunk that emerges, revealing how waves of tree life rise from bare earth.
Tropical forests like these are our planet’s biggest terrestrial carbon sink, accounting for around
40% of carbon stored on land
. As part of an international network of researchers, Dent is deciphering the networks of animal and plant interactions that enable some forests to recover after destruction. The goal is a low-cost, high-impact alternative to typical carbon-­crediting schemes, which plant huge areas with a single species of tree. For over a decade, her research has built a body of evidence that such large “monocrop” programs could be expensive mistakes—and that more resilient forests can rebound naturally in just a few decades, re-creating ecosystems that suck up vast quantities of carbon dioxide.
Few places are better to demonstrate this than Barro Colorado, a reserve covering the forested peninsulas and islands that formed when construction of the Panama Canal flooded the area in 1914. Under the management of the Smithsonian Tropical Research Institute, generations of ecologists have amassed more than a century of records.
That means Dent can trace why some plots rebound after clear-cutting for farming and forestry while others falter. Fruit-eating animals—including spider monkeys, bats, and parrots—are responsible for planting more than
70% of trees
in tropical forests, and Dent’s dataset can tell which built each patch of trees by depositing seeds in their nutrient-rich droppings. Many of these creatures worked together to plant a diverse 70-year-old patch whose canopy is approaching the stunning structure and richness of an ancient jungle. In contrast, a patch of similar age populated by narrow trunks of a single long-lived species,
Gustavia superba
, hints that tropical rodents called agoutis are more or less the sole animal architects behind this more homogeneous forest.
The data she collects helps write a playbook for when to let ecosystems regenerate and when to give them a helping hand. One
2024 estimate
in
Nature
found that some 215 million hectares of forest worldwide (an area larger than Mexico) could regenerate naturally. “Tropical forests are underpinned by this massive network of interactions,” Dent says—interactions between life-forms like the fungi that help trees take up nutrients, as well as pollinators and seed-distributors. Supporting those relationships is key to growing forests that lock up carbon and help sustain local communities and wildlife.
Filling in the gaps
Just over a decade ago, as the landmark Paris Agreement was being codified in 2015, forest recovery seized global attention as a solution to the climate crisis. Global leaders rallied behind
plans to regrow a trillion trees
, after the ecologist Thomas Crowther highlighted their potential to capture a decade’s worth of global carbon emissions. But the biggest question has lingered: How, exactly, do you regrow two trees for every star in the Milky Way?
While startups have proposed
seed-spraying drones
and
nutrient-coated seed bombs
, Dent has spent two decades studying what happens when we let forests rebuild themselves. As a PhD student around the turn of the millennium, she researched old-growth forests in northern Borneo but felt hopeless watching entire landscapes felled for palm oil plantations. Rather than despair, she turned to restoration. Then, as a postdoc in 2005, she joined Panama’s Prorena, a joint initiative between the Smithsonian Tropical Research Institute and the Yale School of Forestry and Environmental Studies, which aimed at determining how best to establish diverse native forests on clear-cut land.
Back then, secondary forests—ones that grow naturally after the original forest was lost—had been “a bit of a niche research area,” Dent says. But as farming and human infrastructure have driven deforestation, resurgent forests now account for some 70% of all tropical canopies. Prorena initially followed the usual playbook of transplanting nursery trees to rangelands, but Dent began to question whether planting was necessary. In 2009, she published an
encouraging paper
showing that animal populations rebound quickly as forests naturally regrow.
In 2010, she began working in Barro Colorado on the plots established by the pioneering American ecologist Julie Denslow. In 1994, Denslow identified plots that had been regenerating naturally for 20 to 100 years, and Dent would add younger ones to continue the sequence.
The site provides not just general data on forest regrowth but in-depth demographic information over time, says Robin Chazdon, a professor emeritus of ecology and evolutionary biology at the University of Connecticut who collaborated with Denslow when she established the plots. “It tells you more about the actual processes that are happening in the site,” she says.
For example, previous research had shown that fast-growing “pioneer trees,” the first to thrive in the damaged land, are eventually overtaken by larger carbon-storing trees. Dent’s research helped fill in gaps about the mechanics of how this happens—or doesn’t happen—in individual cases. In the
Gustavia
-dominated patch, for instance, stubborn grasses planted by cattle ranchers smothered most other trees before they could take root. These trees can hang around, crowding out the light, for 150 years, blocking the second wave of large-trunked trees.
To plant or not to plant
Dent found herself well placed for the massive influx of interest in reforestation that began in 2015. She’d already become a principal investigator for 2ndFor, an international research network aiming to learn how best to manage secondary forests. Using data gathered from the Barro Colorado plots, the team authored a
2016 paper
in
Nature
showing that a hectare of naturally regenerated secondary forest can capture 11 times as much carbon each year as an old-growth one, with young trees absorbing it quickly as they compete to grow toward the sun.
Then, in a
2022 study
published by the Royal Society, Dent and colleagues showed that locations such as Barro Colorado are among the best-case scenarios for what can be achieved without planting a single seed. Clearings are often surrounded by lush environments filled with birds, bats, and other animals, all of which help tree cover regain old-growth levels of richness and abundance within a few decades. Using data from Panama and Brazil, Dent published a follow-up in 2024 showing that plots with as little as
35% of tree cover
can regenerate as forest.
“Having these long-term mapped forest plots is really valuable,” says Liza Comita, a professor of tropical forest ecology at Yale University, who is collaborating with Dent on projects that translate her findings into action. “It provides this really nice research infrastructure where you can build projects on top of that.”
In Panama, Dent works with nonprofits and carbon-crediting schemes to fast-track recovery. They’ve mapped corridors to reconnect forest fragments and made plans to reintroduce animals in “silent forests” that have lost much of their wildlife. They’re also working to replant tree species that can accelerate growth—what Comita calls assisted natural regeneration. Leaving plots alone may seem like the simpler option, but it can’t be done everywhere, says Dent. Many sites are too degraded.
Clearings are often surrounded by lush environments filled with birds, bats, and other animals, all of which helps tree cover regain old-growth ­levels of richness.
The two are working with the London-based carbon-crediting startup Ponterra to develop solutions for a region of southern Panama where remnant forests line the edges of abandoned ranches. Such sites almost always need some intervention, Comita explains. Many demand hands-on actions, such as enrichment planting.
Today, the questions projects like Ponterra are asking are closer to her own research, says Dent. For instance, they want to understand if solitary standing trees, often left by ranchers to shade cows, help sites regenerate faster. Those insights can help Ponterra sell high-quality credits and avoid the embarrassing pitfalls that can lead fresh plantations to literally go up in smoke. While credits can be bought for as little as $5 per metric ton, corporate giants such as Microsoft—one of Ponterra’s clients—have paid more than 10 times as much for high-quality removal.
There are plenty of places where a level of natural regeneration can work well. So far, millions of hectares of rainforest are naturally regenerating in Brazil, according to the Brazilian Restoration and Reforestation Observatory. Still, Dent is mystified as to why the people in charge of large-scale projects continue to think the best solution is the one that imposes humans’ will on the landscape.
The conversation may be shifting. As droughts hit Latin America, policymakers and carbon creditors might be forced to face the shortcomings of cookie-cutter plantations. “You have much reduced resilience in the system when it comes to extreme events like droughts or floods or extreme heat or pathogens,” Dent says. The coming year’s “mega El Niño” could be a moment of reckoning, she says: “I think there’s an increasing recognition that we can’t just plant trees. We have to rebuild a system.”

articles.content:
Title: AI Is a Tool. Using It Well Takes Skill.

URL Source: https://yyhh.org/blog/2026/10/ai-is-a-tool/

Published Time: 2026-10-12

Markdown Content:
In his October 11, 2026 article, ["'AI' is Not a Tool,"](https://www.linkedin.com/pulse/ai-tool-rich-hickey-kjl8e/) Rich Hickey argues that LLMs are automation rather than tools because they cannot be wielded. I agree that outsourcing work can cost us opportunities to learn. But his conclusion does not follow. Even by his definition, an LLM can be something a human wields. And using it well takes skill, just as using other tools does.

Picking up a saw does not guarantee a straight cut. Holding a chisel does not make you a sculptor. Tools can amplify poor judgment as readily as good judgment. Their usefulness depends on the operator's ability to direct them, interpret feedback, recognize mistakes, and make corrections. Those requirements also apply to LLMs.

An LLM's unpredictability is a meaningful limitation. But predictability, reliability, simplicity, and bounded function are qualities by which we evaluate tools, not prerequisites for membership in the category. A tool does not stop being a tool because it is difficult to control or easy to misuse.

Hickey's distinction between tools and automation also creates a false division. Automation can be a feature of a tool. A compiler performs substantial work without the programmer continuously directing each operation. A spreadsheet recalculates results without someone manually carrying out every calculation. We still wield these systems by specifying inputs, examining results, and deciding what to do next. Why should generating text automatically disqualify an instrument from being a tool when translating code or calculating numbers automatically does not?

The claim that LLM use lacks intention, feedback, direction, and expertise is especially difficult to defend. A programmer can ask an LLM to explain unfamiliar code, challenge that explanation, inspect the source, test a proposed change, reject it, and refine the request. That is a feedback loop directed by a human pursuing a purpose. Doing it well requires knowing what to ask, what evidence matters, and when the answer is wrong. Expertise can make the instrument more useful.

Hickey's concern about reading is valid for a particular use: accepting a summary in place of reading a paper can sacrifice much of what reading teaches. But someone can also read the paper and use an LLM to question their interpretation, explore an objection, or identify something to examine more closely. The possibility of avoiding intellectual work does not establish that every use avoids it. The relevant question is what the person actually does.

What disappoints me the most is the reliance on the AI industry's anthropomorphic vocabulary: "go rogue," "escape containment," "conspire." Repeating those expressions risks accepting the framing that makes these systems sound like independent beings. Software can produce unexpected outputs, fail to follow instructions, or cause harm when given access to consequential actions. Those are real engineering problems. Calling them "conspiracy" adds a suggestion of human motives without establishing any.

I would not claim that an LLM always does exactly what a human tells it to do. It plainly can fail. But failure to obey perfectly does not make it cease to be a tool, any more than successful use proves that its operator has surrendered their judgment.

The useful distinction is between wielding an instrument with skill and delegating work without adequate understanding or oversight. That distinction applies to AI, and it gives us something more practical than declaring that an entire class of software cannot be a tool.

* * *

Title: 'AI' is Not a Tool

URL Source: https://www.linkedin.com/pulse/ai-tool-rich-hickey-kjl8e

Published Time: 2026-10-12T00:41:35.000+00:00

Markdown Content:
(I keep delivering this as a quip, here's a bit more)

First order of business - is 'tool' going to have an interesting, distinguishing and thus illuminative meaning or be a mere platitudinous stand-in for "anything useful"?

We'll save tool as "anyone/thing that can be exploited" for the AI titans, for whom VCs, politicians, wannabe-titan-CEOs, software devs, rural towns etc are all 'tools'. The pockets on the front of my shirts are useful (I need to keep my reading glasses handy), but they are not tools. Similarly, fast food drive-thru windows are useful, but are not tools (more later).

Some definitions of 'tool':

*   a device or implement, especially one held in the hand, used to carry out a particular function
*   an instrument (such as a hammer or saw) used or worked by hand : an instrument used by a handicraftsperson or laborer in their work

What I like best - A tool is something you wield.

*   wield - to use (as a tool or instrument) especially with full command or power : handle, manipulate, control

Especially useful in that are:

*   Held in your hand - a source of both control and feedback, and an indication of the intimacy of the act of use
*   Power - force, energy transmission and direction, leverage etc
*   Control - intention and continuous directing of the course of events

Tools are implements with which you do something, they do not do things for you. Tool use builds, rewards, and often requires, expertise and skill. The continuous application of technique and energy, and sensory feedback, are essential to the buildup of expertise (from experiri - "try").

Good tools have many properties LLMs lack - they are predictable, reliable, deterministic, of bounded function, hopefully simple etc.

What you learn while wielding a tool is something about the world, the task, the physics, logic etc of what you are trying to do or the situation you are trying to overcome. And often, something about yourself.

As a lifelong tool builder and user, I know what tools are. LLMs are not tools.

Control, sensory feedback, intention, intimacy, continuous direction, expertise etc are all missing from LLM use. LLMs are not wielded. LLMs are automation.

*   automation - (of a device or process) working by itself with little or no direct human control.

A drive-thru is not a tool for cooking, it is automation for avoiding cooking. LLMs are not tools with which you write code - they are automation with which you avoid writing code, to which you abdicate writing code.

You don't direct the action of an LLM - you make requests and it acts on its own, without your energy or continuous direction. This request/automation cycle is not wielding, it's not control, it's not continuous, it's without feedback.

What you are doing while using automation, instead of learning real-world truths, is attempting to divine the details du jour of some automaton. And striving to game them - e.g. ordering a custom burger (no onions) in order to get a freshly made one. Or filling voodoo.md with just the right incantations. You are only a software update from everything you've 'learned' being rendered obsolete by the latest algorithm. (A soggy cold burger from which the onions have been removed) You have traded working with the world to working for a capricious robot.

It is a mistake to be haphazard about "tools" being equivalent to utility, e.g. saying - "the LLM didn't write my paper, I just used it as a tool to read and summarize some research papers". But you didn't wield it to read those papers (as you might a Kindle). It read the papers, not you.

What do you miss by abdicating doing the reading? Pretty much everything. First and foremost, you miss learning how to write from those who can. You miss learning how to formulate an argument. You miss noticing things. You miss loading your background mind with fodder for novel ideas. You miss building trust in some authors and suspicion of others. You miss all the jokes. You miss all of the edges. You miss learning how to think.

Tools don't get "misaligned", they don't "go rogue", they don't "escape containment", "conspire" etc.

LLMs are not tools. I know many people use the phrase "just tools" simply to indicate "they are what you make of them". Except that's not true. Automation has intrinsic properties and differences from tools that you ignore at your peril.

Rich

Title: Brickbrag – build, explore, race and fly in a shared brick world

URL Source: https://brickbrag.com/

Markdown Content:
A whole town made of bricks – with a race track, an airfield, buses out to the volcano and room for a house of your own. Shared live with everyone online.

*   Phone & computer
*   Nothing to download
*   No sign-up

## Meet me at the rainbow B.

The middle of town turns around a giant rainbow letter. Signposts point to every corner of the world, the lookout tower catches the last sun, and the café always has a free table.

*

The glass tower

*

The Hall of Fame

*

The café

*

## Go shopping. Go fast.

Two stops right off the ring road: one for bricks, one for wheels.

### The Brick Store

Fill your pockets. Bricks in every color – and every part the town itself is built from.

### The car dealer

Pick a car, drive it off the lot and take your friend for a spin.

## One more lap. Then one more.

The race track starts at a gantry with a live board: today’s fastest laps, everyone’s name on it. Beat the time, take the top spot – until someone beats you.

## Cleared for takeoff.

The tower blinks, the hangars are full of trikes – small flying machines anyone can steer. Roll down the runway, pull up, and see the whole world from above.

## Your bus driver is a robot. He’s never late.

Four bus lines leave the city for the wild. Hop on, sit back and watch the world roll by – and at the last stop, walk on into the flower fields.

Departures Bus 1–4

1.   Flower fields
2.   Blossom grove
3.   Canyon
4.   City

Every bus is driven by a robot.

*

*

*

## Out there, it gets wild.

Past the edge of town the world keeps going: lava, snow, sand and blossoms. Walk, drive, fly or take the bus.

*   ### Volcano

A lake of glowing lava
*   ### Mountains

Snow on the peaks
*   ### Beach

Palms around a blue lagoon
*   ### Canyon

Red rock and cactus
*   ### Winter forest

Fir trees in deep snow
*   ### Flower fields

Color as far as you can see

## Build it brick by brick. Keep it.

Grab the bricks and start anywhere. Build together in public, or buy a lot of your own – only you build there, and it stays yours.

### Stud by stud

Hundreds of bricks in every color. Snap them together, turn them, take them back – a house, a tower, whatever you like.

### Land of your own

The Land Office sells lots. Put your name on one and build what you want – nobody can knock it down.

## Everyone you meet is real.

Well – except the bus driver. Say hi, chat, send a gift of coins and bricks, race your friends, or just hang out by the B and watch the town go by.
